title: Former school IT worker charged with grooming, school says
text:
A former IT support technician who worked at Williamstown High School in Melbourne's south-west has been charged with criminal offences relating to grooming and trafficking, the school says.

In a letter to parents seen by the ABC, principal Giorgio Catalano has advised families of "concerning news" regarding former IT contractor Mario Stocki.

"Mario has been charged with criminal offences relating to grooming, and trafficking and supplying a drug of dependence to a child," he wrote.

"The charges relate to former students at our school."

Mr Stocki worked at the government school's Bayview (for years 7 to 9) and Pasco (years 10 to 12) campuses between October 2012 and May 2024, the letter said.

"As a result of these charges, Mario is not currently permitted to work in any Victorian school or any other place requiring a working with children clearance," Mr Catalano wrote.

Principal Giorgio Catalano requested that parents have discretion out of respect for anyone who might be directly involved. (School website)

"There is no evidence to suggest the alleged offending relates to any other students of our school but given the nature of the charges I wanted to ensure you were informed of this concerning matter directly by me."

Mr Catalano directed parents and carers to resources on child safety and said he was available to be contacted about any questions at any time.

"As this matter is before the court, I am unable to provide further information currently," he wrote.

He asked parents to use their discretion when discussing the matter "out of respect for the privacy, safety and wellbeing of any person directly impacted".

The Victorian Education Department issued a brief statement on Tuesday evening.

"These charges are deeply distressing," a spokesperson said.

"Williamstown High School families have been informed of the charges and of supports available to them."

Technology firm says Stocki worked in schools this year

Education technology firm LWT systems, which supplies technology services to schools across Australia, told the ABC that Mr Stocki worked for the company from April to June this year.

"He worked across a number of schools in Melbourne's western suburbs, carrying out laptop repairs," Ian Doherty from LWT Systems said.

"This was a technical repair role and did not involve unsupervised contact with students."

Mr Doherty said Mr Stocki advised the company on June 25 that he expected to lose his Working with Children Check.

"As his role involved working in schools, maintaining a current Working with Children Check was an essential condition of his employment," he said.

"LWT therefore ended his employment.

"At the time, LWT was not aware of the charges against Mr Stocki.

"We have only now become aware of the allegations through publicly available media reports and are deeply concerned by their nature."

Victoria Police has been contacted for comment.

title: Marnus Labuschagne suffers bizarre Shield dismissal
text:
Marnus Labuschagne's frustrating run of starts has hit a bizarre new level, with the dropped Test star caught off the back of his bat against NSW in the Sheffield Shield.

Labuschagne was out for 34 before tea on day three in Sydney, with Queensland 2-106 and an 81-run lead when rain stopped play.

Ryan Hicks's fighting 92 not out for the Blues on Tuesday morning and Sydney's wet weather means a result is unlikely, with Test ramifications now the bigger factor.

But Labuschagne's dismissal was the big moment on day three, before rain washed away close to two hours of play.

After a long run of scores between 30 and 49 for Australia in the past year, Labuschagne was out for 37 and 34 in this match.

He was attempting to sweep Lyon when the ball bounced off his upper chest and onto the back of his bat before being well caught by Hicks.

Labuschagne pointed to his chest in frustration as he argued the ball had not come off his bat, but replays told a different story.

The wicket was also a notable one for Lyon (1-30), who took 1-86 in the first innings and looked largely unthreatening in Queensland's first innings on a docile SCG pitch.

National selectors have shown over the past 15 months they are no longer guaranteed to play a spinner in every Test, having gone into five of the past 11 without one.

Lyon will be in Australia's squad for the first Test against New Zealand in Perth on December 9, with his role as the side's number one spinner not up for debate.

But if it is a pace-friendly wicket, questions could be raised around his spot.

Lyon took a fourth-innings 3-51 to help NSW to victory in their last match against South Australia and more wickets on Wednesday will not hurt his cause.

NSW resumed at 7-195 in reply to Queensland's first-innings 278 on Tuesday and were 8-197 when Lyon fell early.

Hicks then put on 59 for the ninth wicket with Liam Hatcher and 47 for the last with Bryce Jackson, pulling quick Michael Neser and Tom Straker for sixes.

Hatcher then had Angus Lovell caught at midwicket for four, as the Blues eyed off running through Queensland to force a result.

But Hugo Burdon ensured Queensland kept the match under control, hitting Jackson for two sixes over the legside on his way to an unbeaten 53.

Mitchell Swepson provided the other highlight for Queensland, taking NSW's last three wickets to finish with a career-best 6-73.

Swepson has not been part of a Test squad since Australia's last tour of India, but remains the number one red-ball legspinner if required.

AAP

title: Lani Pallister eyes history as bullish Aussies lay down Olympic gauntlet
text:
Australia's swimmers are bullishly approaching the 2026 World Short Course Championships as they gear up for a massive lead-in to the 2028 LA Olympics.

The 23-strong Australian team heads to Beijing on Thursday, ahead of the short course championships getting underway on December 1.

Lani Pallister will headline the Australian team, looking to win a third consecutive women's 800-metre title, an event she also holds the world record in, beating legendary American Katie Ledecky's mark by a colossal 3.42 seconds in October last year.

"Any time I get behind the blocks I want to make history; I want to swim times that haven't been seen before," she said.

"I was super stoked last year with my 800. Breaking Katie's world record by three seconds was, I feel, the big jumping point for my career, particularly in the last 12 months."

Lani Pallister handed Katie Ledecky a rare defeat in California. (Getty Images: Maddie Meyer)

For a generation, Ledecky has been the benchmark against which all other female distance swimmers are measured — and for good reason.

The American legend has proven almost unbeatable over the 800m freestyle, claiming the last four Olympic gold medals in the distance.

And yet, at the Pan Pacific Championships earlier this year, Pallister stunned the living legend to land a remarkable psychological blow as the Olympics approaches.

"I am the kind of person who likes getting behind the blocks and racing everyone," Pallister said.

"I don't want the result to be just about beating Katie; I want it to be [that] I swam a world-class time that only two other people in history have beaten.

"That's a really important thing for me, stamping my legacy as a distance swimmer and not just someone that's racing someone else in the pool."

Pallister acknowledges that Ledecky's mantle as the greatest women's distance swimmer of all time is unlikely to be shaken in the short or even medium term, whether she claims victory in LA or not.

But that does not mean that the Sunshine Coast swimmer is overawed by her rival.

Lani Pallister is planning on getting through a mountain of work. (Getty Images: Maddie Meyer)

"Katie's held that title [greatest of all time] for the last 14 years. I think she's done absolutely tremendous things for women's distance swimming and women's sport in general," Pallister said.

"Just to be part of that story and part of that race in two years' time will be unreal, but also knowing that I'm doing it for me and because I want to swim and I want to be successful.

"To be able to have the opportunity to race in two years' time and be in Brisbane in six years' time and challenge for Olympic gold medals and be close to world records for long course and short course is all I ever dreamed of."

Pallister is a noted workaholic when it comes to racing — the day after the trials for the world short course championships she flew from Sydney to Brisbane to compete in an ocean swim hosted by her surf lifesaving club, Alex Heads. She won it, too.

As such, the 24-year-old will endure an abundance of racing over the next 12 months, which is the backbone of her strategy for success.

"Racing's the best form of training," Pallister said of her plans over the next year.

"So I'm the type of person who's happy to live out of a suitcase and travel and see friends and people overseas, but more importantly get the race practice in."

Flynn Southam has also embraced the chance to race hard and often over the past 12 months, enjoying huge success in Glasgow at the Commonwealth Games.

Flynn Southam says Australia is in a golden era for swimming. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

"I think it kind of stamped my authority," Southam said of his four golds and one silver in Glasgow.

"Not just as potential, but, 'He's here and he's arrived.'

"Our job is to go into the Americans' backyard and play some games with them."

Southam even went as far as to say Australia was in a "golden age" of swimming, a bold claim for a nation with such a tremendous history in the pool.

"This is the best team we've had in this Olympic cycle, and probably will be going into LA [the best] that we've ever had," the 21-year-old said.

Southam, the Commonwealth 100m freestyle champion, said the prospect of competing in LA was all-consuming, dominating his thoughts.

"It's all I can think about," he said.

"Most people can go down to the pub and watch a game of sport and switch off.

"But for me, it's all I think about; it's in my mind 24/7.

"That's what fuels my fire. I live for it. I breathe this stuff.

"The higher the challenge, the higher the pressure, the more I rise to the occasion.

"I think the man who's going to win the 100 free at the LA Olympic Games is the one who is going to be able to deal with the most pressure, the most adversity and still perform under any circumstances.

"And I believe with my whole heart that that's going to be me."

title: Business owner banned from employing migrants
text:
An Adelaide business owner has been banned from employing migrant workers for three years, with a union saying a public register of approved visa sponsors would help public oversight of potential worker exploitation.

Viet Quoc Mai, who operates the Mr Viet restaurant in Adelaide CBD, has this week been banned from employing temporary migrant workers.

The NSW-based operator of another hospitality group sanctioned in an unrelated exploitation case was also handed a similar ban.

In 2025, the Federal Court ordered Mai to pay back $407,546 owed to 36 underpaid workers. He and his wife were also ordered to pay a combined $395,000 in additional court penalties.

The court found the underpaid workers were casually employed, primarily international students from Vietnam, and in some cases were paid as little as $15 per hour.

Wages owed ranged from $75 to $58,592, according to the Fair Work Ombudsman.

Mai is now listed on the government's Prohibited Employer Register and will be unable to employ migrant workers until his ban ends on November 19, 2029.

Public oversight register to help transparency

In May, a report published by the Migrant Justice Institute found two thirds of migrant workers could be underpaid, and that international students could be collectively underpaid more than $3.1 billion annually.

More than a third may also be paid below the national minimum wage, the report found.

The Department of Home Affairs recently released new resources for employers and migrant workers, including multilingual guides on reporting worker exploitation and on how to access help.

John Taylor, Commander of Field Operations and Sponsor Monitoring at the Australian Border Force (ABF), said his officers were "actively identifying and investigating employers who are doing the wrong thing, and those who exploit migrant workers should be on notice".

The ABF said it continues to investigate cases of potential migrant worker exploitation. (AAP: Dan Peled)

SA Unions want the federal government to expedite the introduction of transparency and public oversight measures, such as a register of approved worker visa sponsors as provided for in anti-exploitation legislation that took effect in October.

That legislation allows a register to be published listing approved sponsors, their ABN and postcode, the number of sponsored workers and their occupations.

A spokesperson said SA Unions was "looking forward to Home Affairs using these new powers to make a public register a reality".

"A public register which increases transparency around which employers are sponsoring migrant workers, and in which roles, will be an important resource for making sure workplace rights information and assistance can get to where it’s needed most," the spokesperson said.

ABC News has approached Mr Mai for comment.

title: Massive illegal fishing bust in northern waters alarms industry
text:
Border officials say a massive illegal fishing bust made in Australia's northern waters could potentially be the largest apprehension of its kind in the nation's history.

A foreign fishing vessel allegedly carrying more than 25 tonnes of fish product was apprehended by the Australian Border Force (ABF) on the Arafura Sea last week.

The crew was taken to Darwin for further investigation.

ABF said it could be the biggest apprehension of its kind ever, as the boat was allegedly equipped with commercial-scale fishing equipment, such as a gillnet, and advanced navigational systems.

It is suspected to have been operating illegally within Australia's Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) in the Arafura Sea.

ABF said officers boarded the foreign boat following a "pursuit" at sea, which took authorities outside the EEZ and into international waters.

A map of the Australian Fishing Zone showing where fishing is allowed in the Timor and Arafura seas. (Supplied: Australian Fisheries Management Authority)

While charges have not been laid, ABF Deputy Commander Ranjeev Maharaj said the seizure represented "a significant operational outcome".

"This vessel is a sophisticated commercial fishing platform capable of spending extended periods at sea and harvesting industrial-scale quantities of marine resources," he said.

"Unlike the smaller illegal foreign fishing vessels more commonly encountered in northern Australia, this vessel was capable of extended offshore operations, carrying large quantities of catch and supporting commercial-scale fishing activity."

Authorities say the foreign crew failed to comply with directions to stop. (Supplied: Australian Border Force)

An escalating issue

Grant Barker from Northern Wildcatch Seafood has been fishing in Australia's far northern waters for over 20 years and said the scale of the vessel and its alleged activity was "next level" and a real concern.

"It's quite an alarming step-up in terms of sophistication of vessel and catching efficiency," he said.

"This boat is next level and the first time we've seen a boat with this sort of power in our waters."

Grant Barker has been commercially fishing in Australia's northern waters for more than 20 years. (ABC Landline: Chris Lewis)

Mr Barker said he had seen other foreign fishing vessels take only "a few hundred kilograms" of fish product from Australian waters.

"To actually catch a boat with 25 tonnes of product on board is a big step up and big move by whoever is behind this and financing [this vessel]," he said.

Mr Barker said he recently encountered six motorised foreign fishing vessels near Browse Island, 450 kilometres off the coast from Broome.

He said the incursion of foreign boats was likely impacting fish stocks.

"I think [authorities] are doing a very good job trying to get on top of this, but it would be good to see the Commonwealth government get behind them with some serious funding, because it just gets worse year on year," he said.

"And one of the big issue is our penalties are too soft.

"They should be burning every single vessel they catch in our waters, and the guys on the boats should be jailed."

The foreign fishing vessel pictured alongside two Cape-class patrol boats operated by Border Force and the Navy. (Supplied: Australian Border Force)

A joint media statement published by Border Force and the Australian Fisheries Management Authority (AFMA) said the vessel's "disposal" would be determined in accordance with Australian law.

The ABC understands the boat is currently moored in Darwin Harbour.

AFMA was contacted for comment.

title: Australia's most affordable city masking a 'two-tier' rental system: expert
text:
Once considered one of Australia's most unaffordable cities for renters, Canberra is now out in front when it comes to rental affordability.

The latest Rental Affordability Index has found Canberra to have the most "acceptable" rental market of Australia's capital cities, with the average renting household spending 22.6 per cent of its income on rent.

It is a marked improvement for the nation's capital, which was considered the second most unaffordable city for renters back in 2022.

Perth currently holds the title of having the least affordable rental market, followed by Hobart and Sydney.

So why has Canberra's rental market improved while other cities have seen a decline?

Canberra remains one of two capital cities in the country classed as "acceptable" in terms of rental affordability. (ABC News: Alexandra Beech)

Rental caps could be working

The study, by CGS Economics and Planning and National Shelter, measures rental affordability relative to household incomes, and found the ACT has the highest average rental household gross income at $142,658 per year.

SGS Economics principal Ellen Witte said comparatively high average incomes had kept pace with rent increases in Canberra, partly due to rent stabilisation measures introduced by the ACT government in 2019.

Rent increases in Canberra can only happen once a year with eight weeks' notice, and they are capped at 10 per cent above the increase in the Consumer Price Index.

"There are some guardrails now ... and so it's still possible as a landlord to increase your rents, but not in an excessive way," Ms Witte said.

Ellen Witte says the ACT is "bucking the national trend" when it comes to housing affordability. (ABC News: Sebastian Baltyn)

The high incomes and targeted policy have helped buffer Canberra from declines seen in other jurisdictions like Hobart and Perth, Ms Witte said.

"Out of the seven capital cities in Australia, five are tracking very poorly — where even the average income household is now struggling to pay rent — and only two are getting better," she said.

" Canberra is getting better [and] Melbourne is stabilising, and it just happens to be so that those are the two jurisdictions that put in place some regulations around rent increases. "

Corinne Dobson says more affordable housing is needed to ensure lower-income Canberrans aren't priced out of a home. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

Unaffordable for low-income renters

While Canberra may be considered the most affordable city for renters overall, it remains unaffordable for low-income earners and students.

ACT Shelter chief executive Corinne Dobson said the positive headline figures "only tell half of the story", with Canberra's high average incomes masking a "two-tier" rental system.

"We do see really high rates of rental stress, and that's because the rental market is more pitched towards the average income and people on average incomes in the ACT are earning a lot more than elsewhere," she said.

" But if you're someone who's on a lower income, if you're on income support, or maybe you're in early childhood education and care or in hospitality, it is really tough finding an affordable rental in the ACT. "

Canberra remains unaffordable for many low-income renters and students. (ABC News: Mark Moore)

The study found people who worked in hospitality and rented in the ACT were spending an average of 38 per cent of their income on rent, while early childhood educators were spending 37 per cent.

A person on JobSeeker payments and rental assistance in Canberra sees 99 per cent of their income go to rent, while median rents were taking up 62 per cent of a single pensioner's aged pension income.

"For people on the lowest incomes, we do see the highest rates of rental stress here in Canberra, and that's been the case for well over a decade and it continues to be the case," Ms Dobson said.

Dylan Adams has spent months searching for an affordable rental to share with two other friends. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

For students, like Dylan Adams, Canberra's rental market has been proving incredibly difficult; he has been looking for a new place for months.

"The houses that are more affordable for students usually have one or two or many issues with them, whether it's mould in the bathrooms, or there aren't enough bathrooms, or the quality of the kitchen is poor," he said.

He is now considering a second job on top of his studies so he can afford to pay a higher rent.

"I'm looking at upping the amount of days that I work next year and potentially harming my studies to have enough money to rent a house that at least is a good enough quality that I feel like I can live in it properly," he said.

Low-income renters 'between a rock and a hard place'

Ms Witte said many tenants in Canberra were "between a rock and a hard place".

"What we see is parents skipping meals, at least then their children can eat; people skipping medicine, people turning homeless — even people with jobs are sometimes now living out of their cars," she said.

"Apart from financial hardship, there's a lot of social and psychological impacts.

"The fact that people can't participate in a whole range of activities anymore, children that can't participate in sports and things like that, is really affecting people's lives in so many ways."

Dylan Adams says housing that is more affordable for students often has issues like mould in the bathrooms. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

That is something Mr Adams has experienced first-hand.

"Often it's a big joke for young people when they're renting houses to have two-minute noodle dinners every single night because their rent is so incredibly high that it's taking out a majority of their pay," he said.

title: Suncorp accused of 'making a mockery' of people's pain as profit culture exposed
text:
Multi-billion-dollar insurance giant Suncorp has been accused of a "toxic" corporate culture that incentivises staff to deny home insurance claims.

Warning: This story discusses self-harm.

Former claims investigator Ashley Austin alleges that she was rewarded for increasing company profits by reducing the value of claims, at the expense of customers.

"It was a culture where we were encouraged to meet a monetary target," Ms Austin told 7.30.

"Whoever can decline the most amount of claims by Friday, 3pm, we'll give you [a] $50 gift card."

The whistleblower says it was done to keep profits rolling in and claims processing slow.

"This was how profits were made," she said.

"Trying to keep policies active, obtain the premiums monthly, yearly, and then when it comes time to making a claim, make it too hard."

After five years at Suncorp, and while on parental leave last year, Ms Austin decided she could not return to the company.

"I inflicted a lot of pain on people for monetary gain and that didn't sit right with me, I couldn't do it anymore," she told 730.

In the last financial year, Suncorp sold more than $15 billion in insurance premiums across its brands. (ABC NEWS: Lucas Hill)

Several other former Suncorp employees detailed similar practices to 7.30.

"It's toxic and misleading," Ms Austin told 7.30.

"They are not there to provide assistance to Australians or families in need," she said, "It's all about profit, making money, business."

Suncorp and its subsidiaries provide insurance to millions of Australians. Those companies collected more than $15 billion in insurance premiums in the last financial year.

Suncorp made more than $1 billion in profit, which it put down to "disciplined cost management and revenue growth".

Suncorp declined an interview with 7.30.

In a statement, its spokesperson said the insurer takes allegations insurance claims are "deliberately and improperly declined, delayed or minimised extremely seriously".

"Such behaviour would be contrary to our culture, policies, training and legal and regulatory obligations," the statement read.

'Making a mockery' of people's pain

The corporate tactics allegedly used at Suncorp could have devastating consequences for its customers trying to fix their damaged homes.

Ms Austin says customers would contact her distressed by the lengthy delays, confusing processes and insufficient funds to pay their claims.

"People that were just crying out for help after we stripped them of any dignity that they had," she said.

In a work group chat seen by 7.30 Suncorp staff joked about how they would handle customer concerns.

A work group chat of Suncorp employees joking about how they respond to customer concerns. (ABC News: Bill McGuire )

"There was laughing and references to the type of scripted responses we would use when people express their hardships to us," Ms Austin said.

"Making a mockery of it."

Ms Austin said customers would sometimes threaten suicide over the stress of their experience with Suncorp.

"We would back people into a corner where they felt as though they had no choice but to end their life, or felt they were so mentally impacted that they could not continue," she said.

She told 7.30 that she was desensitised to the issues at the time and would request more documentation, which would delay the claim.

"We would ask for a clearance from their psychiatrist or treating medical professionals ... and use that and say, 'We can't move forward until you provide that document to us'."

A Suncorp spokesperson said the insurer has dedicated support for customers experiencing vulnerability.

"Customers do not need to provide proof of a mental health condition to access that support, and it does not impact their claim."

After resigning Ms Austin filed a complaint about Suncorp’s corporate practices with insurance regulator ASIC.

She said she is now living through what it's like for a customer, after having to lodge her own claim with a different provider in May this year.

"What I have experienced in my own claim are the exact same practices that I inflicted on customers as an investigator myself," she said.

KPIs could be in breach of the law

The corporate regulator ASIC is responsible for stamping out systemic problems in the insurance industry, and has powers to penalise providers that breach their legal duties to uphold consumer protections.

While ASIC did not confirm if it is investigating Suncorp, its Commissioner Alan Kirkland says it relies on customers or employees to report their concerns.

ASIC commissioner Alan Kirkland says setting KPIs to reduce the value of claims could be in breach of the law. (ABC News: Adam Wyatt)

"That's the sort of intelligence that feeds into the decisions we make about the sorts of investigations we pursue and ultimately some of the matters that we take through the courts," Mr Kirkland said.

He warned insurers that are setting business targets around reducing the value of claims could be "in breach of the law".

"It is very clear that insurers have to go about their business efficiently, honestly, and fairly," he said.

" If they're setting incentives or KPIs for their staff that conflict with that obligation ... they should expect ASIC to consider taking action. "

The 'vulnerable claimant'

Emma Silberstein is a Suncorp customer who has been navigating a home insurance claim for almost three years.

Emma Silberstein has been dealing with an ongoing home insurance claim for nearly three years. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

She lodged the claim with Suncorp's subsidiary AAMI after her house in regional Victoria was flooded by a storm just after Christmas, 2023.

Her home still hasn't been repaired, and isn’t safe to live in due to mould contamination.

Emma Silberstein's property in regional Victoria was impacted by storm damage. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

"It's like mourning or grieving something that I can't let go of, but I also can't move on," Ms Silberstein told 7.30.

Do you know more? If you have more information about this investigation, you can securely contact reporter Adelaide Miller at miller.adelaide@proton.me

Despite Suncorp sending multiple assessors and contractors to Ms Silberstein's home after the storm, it took six months for the company to outline the work needed to fix the damage.

"I couldn't understand why the delays were so severe without adequate response as to what was actually happening," she said.

By then mould had spread throughout her property, with an assessment confirming "high concentrations" in the bedroom and ensuite.

Loading

The latter recorded a spore count almost 160 times the outdoor control sample.

Ms Silberstein told Suncorp the stress of her claim had forced her to take leave from work, and her file was updated to reflect her status as a 'vulnerable claimant'.

In July 2024, the insurer moved Ms Silberstein into temporary accommodation, and offered her a cash settlement of about $70,000 to fix her property and replace her damaged contents.

Delays in repairs caused mould contamination in Emma's home and on her contents. (Supplied: Emma Silberstein)

But an alternative quote she obtained estimated repairs alone could cost $190,000.

She has lodged 10 separate complaints with the insurer but only two have been investigated.

"No matter how I tried to tackle it, there wasn't ever a justice system available internally that would rectify what's happened here," she said.

In April 2025, AAMI's internal complaints department acknowledged the insurer had failed to control the mould. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

In April 2025, Suncorp's internal complaints department acknowledged the insurer had failed to control the mould, increased its cash settlement offer for her contents by about $20,000 and compensated her for her experience.

She says the amount was still not enough to repair the damage.

"It would've covered a fraction of the works that were required," she said.

"Three years later ... I'm left with a partial strip out quote that will do absolutely nothing towards returning the home to what it was."

After her temporary accommodation funded by Suncorp ended last year, she has been living between her mum's place and sleeping in her garden.

Ms Silberstein says she sometimes sleeps in her swag. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

An old bus becomes a new home

After losing hope with her claims process and desperate for secure housing, Ms Silberstein has taken matters into her own hands and bought an old bus to live in.

Emma Silberstein is turning an old bus into a temporary home. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

"I have looked at every avenue to be able to return here ... but my intention is to renovate it completely."

"The bus provides eventually, hopefully a safer place to live."

She lodged a complaint with the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA) in April, but it took nearly six months for the agency to call her.

She says Suncorp has crushed her belief that insurers are there to protect people.

The inside of the bus that Ms Silberstein is renovating. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

"It's not just keeping costs low, it is destroying so many facets of what makes an individual," she said.

"Then claimants have to figure out how to rebuild, not just their homes, not just recollecting possessions, but a whole identity."

Ms Austin says she wants insurers like Suncorp to be held accountable for their conduct.

"This is an industry that has been swept under the carpet for way too long, and I don't think anyone can quite grasp the concept of how these businesses are running," she said.

" They try to sell themselves as helping ... no, they're not. They're there to make money. "

title: Job losses feared after $20m slashed from Victorian specialist schools
text:
A Victorian alternative school is facing significant job cuts as part of a federal government funding crackdown that has cut about $20 million from its budget.

The ABC understands special assistance school group Saints College, which operates seven campuses across Melbourne and regional Victoria, has had its funding slashed as part of the government's crackdown on the Nationally Consistent Collection of Data on School Students with Disability scheme (NCCD).

A source connected to the school said they feared more than 100 jobs out of 500 across the state would be cut, which would have a significant impact on students.

"These are the most vulnerable young people who have been brought in with an amazing opportunity to excel," they said.

"If this school falls over, it will be terrible … with [students having] nowhere to go."

The federal budget included a focus on "compliance activities" in the government's school spending, including new mechanisms it said would ensure funding was directed based on need while closing regulatory loopholes.

Saints College, previously known as St Joseph's Schools, works with students aged 12 to 25, offering free education to some of the state's most vulnerable and marginalised children, as well as free meals and wellbeing support.

It has campuses in North Melbourne, Geelong, Colac, Ballarat, Bungaree, Sunshine and Fitzroy North, all of which are run by Catholic organisation Edmund Rice Education Australia.

In a statement, Saints College executive principal Michael Crowe said the federal government recently completed an audit on the way "they assess public funding in specialist assistance schools".

"Following a detailed review of the significant changes, Saints College campuses in Ballarat and Bungaree are in the process of restructuring some roles which will ensure no programs are shut," Mr Crowe said.

"Our commitment to front-line teaching staff remains our absolute priority."

It is not clear how many teaching positions will be affected by the forecast cuts, or whether other campuses will be affected.

"There will also be a restructure at a senior management level that will ensure Saints College maintains equitable leadership across all programs statewide," the source said.

A spokesperson for the federal Education department said all schools were required to provide "reasonable adjustments for children and young people with disability so they can access and participate in education on the same basis as students without disability".

"The Department of Education undertakes an annual program to validate information reported by selected schools about student enrolments and attributes," the spokesperson said.

"Where the department finds insufficient evidence to substantiate school reporting, it may be subject to recovery."

title: ABC to discontinue a TV channel and pursue YouTube content creation
text:
The ABC will discontinue its ABC Entertains channel and aggressively pursue content generation for YouTube.

The decision was announced as part of the ABC strategy update for 2027.

ABC managing director Hugh Marks said the public broadcaster will focus on pursuing distinctive, live and local "content themes".

"Being distinctive ultimately means best in class, it means excellence, it means standing out, it means memorable," Mr Marks said.

"That's going to be very important for how we compete.

"It needs to be original."

Hugh Marks outlined a new strategy of "distinctive, live and local". (ABC News: John Gunn)

As a savings measure, the ABC will eliminate one of its four broadcast television channels, ABC Entertains.

Mr Marks said it was a decision "of significant value for the ABC, in terms of our ability to realise money to be able to invest into the priority areas".

The channel currently runs on free-to-air TV and iview and was originally branded as ABC Me, launching in December 2009.

"ABC Entertains generally is re-runs and acquired programming, and so for me that doesn't fit with the strategy that I just outlined earlier, with distinctive live or local," Mr Marks said.

"Dropping ABC Entertains as a channel under the terms of our transmission agreement with Broadcast Australia enables us to free up potentially tens of millions of dollars per year in savings."

The savings from all measures announced are expected to total "around about $50 million per year of money that we've been able to reallocate from other activities into those priorities that I mentioned before", the MD said.

YouTube push

A key part of the ABC strategy into 2027 is a greater push on the world's biggest video platform, YouTube.

Or as one executive put it, "the 800-pound gorilla in the television world".

Mr Marks said the ABC will be "embracing YouTube as a primary distribution platform going forward".

Changes to the ABC News and Current Affairs division are yet to be announced. (ABC)

The broadcaster sees its audience using YouTube as a "primary experience for their entertainment", Mr Marks said.

"These are audiences that we need to meet in the platforms that they choose and we need to meet them with the content areas that are going to be really good in that environment.

"So obviously that'll be news, that'll be specialist content," Mr Marks said.

"There will be some screen audio on demand video, which is now video on demand as well.

" We will be significantly ramping up the number of channels and content that we publish to YouTube going forward. "

News and current affairs changes 'likely'

The ABC rolled out 76 redundancies in the 2026 financial year and a further 18 since July, alongside the announcement in September of 46 roles to be cut from the Screen division.

Asked if there would be broader cuts in 2027, Mr Marks said, "that is not currently the plan".

The organisation's News and Current Affairs director, Simon Robinson, only took up the role in September, and will announce changes to that division in the first quarter of next year.

"News and Current Affairs, again, their changes are to come next year, so that's premature to [say] that there won't be any changes in News and Current Affairs," Mr Marks said.

" I think Simon's being consistent in saying that there likely will be. "

Radio negotiations, executive changes

The ABC's radio transmission agreement is currently up for renewal. The original contract was negotiated in the late 1990s and ends in 2029.

Mr Marks said the current proposal was for the ABC to extend its radio contract and radio channels.

"We expect again to receive a discount on the transmission arrangements, which I hope would be material, as well to those savings that I'm looking to extract."

The ABC is renegotiating its radio transmission agreements. (Supplied: ABC)

Mr Marks also flagged executive role changes, including Gavin Fang adding oversight of sport to his role as editorial director.

"The creation of a dedicated Sport division reflects the importance the ABC places on sport and our commitment to strengthening our coverage for audiences across the country," the ABC said in a statement.

"The new team will bring together the sport roles in News, Audio and Screen."

Mr Marks said sport should be "a big priority of the ABC".

Jessica Radburn, who is currently the head of Audio on Demand, will also be responsible for coordinating all the off-platform work that happens in all the divisions.

Dina Rosendorff, currently the head of Radio National, will also become head of specialist content for the ABC.

Asked at a media roundtable if either Radio National or News Radio would be restructured, Mr Marks said, "to my mind the three channels, Radio National, News Radio and Local Radio do have distinct and easily identifiable purposes".

This, Mr Marks said, fits in with the ABC's strategy.

"If I think for it as a content proposition and I look at Radio National, it is the depth of expertise and knowledge and things that exist there, and the ability to do really outstanding work in areas that nobody else is really doing."

However, Mr Marks said it would be something the news director, Mr Robinson, would look at.

He said Mr Robinson would consider what was "the best use of his resources across all the different channels".

Mr Robinson said he wanted ABC News to be the go-to organisation for breaking news.

title: Queensland tungsten mine to supply critical mineral to US military
text:
A tungsten mine in Far North Queensland will become a key supplier to the US Department of Defense as part of major expansion plans.

Tungsten is a critical mineral used in heavy machinery and defence manufacturing.

The Mount Carbine mine, west of Cairns, is one of the largest in the world outside of China, which supplies about 80 per cent of the global market.

"Tungsten from [Mount Carbine] will build fighter jets and submarines in the United States," Premier David Crisafulli said.

"So, critical minerals from here protecting the globe and protecting the economic opportunities for North and Far North Queenslanders.

"I actually think we have a duty, a sovereign capability to be a trusted supplier on the world stage."

David Crisafulli speaks at the Mount Carbine Tungsten Mine. (ABC Far North: Brendan Mounter)

The move is seen as part of a broader US push to reduce its reliance on China and other geopolitical rivals for critical minerals used in defence manufacturing.

From January 1, the US government will ban defence contractors from using tungsten sourced from China, Russia, Iran or North Korea.

Delivering to the world

The mine is operated by EQ Resources, which will double its processing capacity under an expansion project due for commissioning next year.

"We'll double our crushing capacity from 1 million to 2 million tonnes, and using the low-grade stockpile, our nameplate capacity will go up by 20 per cent," chief financial officer Jono Kort said.

Mr Kort said the project had been funded by the company itself and would not rely on taxpayer funds.

"We want to be delivering to the western world in terms of critical tungsten, and that is a key product [that] underpins defence, artificial intelligence, EVs, medical and ground engaging tools," he said.

Jono Kort says the expansion project will not rely on taxpayer funds. (ABC Far North: Christopher Testa)

Last year, EQ Resources secured a $US34 million letter of interest from the Export-Import Bank of the United States (EXIM) for the capital expansion and further development of the Mount Carbine Tungsten Mine.

An EXIM letter of interest is a non-binding indication that the bank is willing to consider financing an export deal, subject to further review and a formal application.

Local employment opportunities

The expansion is expected to create 100 direct construction jobs as well as more indirect jobs through local contractors.

State member for Cook David Kempton said it would be good for the local economy.

"Ultimately, there will be about 400 people working here, all drawn from the local area, and it's the multiplier effect that brings so much to this region," Mr Kempton said.

David Kempton, Dale Last and David Crisafulli hold jars of tungsten at the Mount Carbine mine. (ABC Far North: Christopher Testa)

Mr Kort said EQ Resources aimed to employ people who lived within 100 kilometres of the mine.

When asked about ethical concerns regarding the mine expansion, Mr Crisafulli said there was a market that needed to be met.

"We have a responsibility to meet that market, and we are a trusted supplier and a trusted partner, and the US is a really big part of that," he said.

title: Qld health minister says families ‘want answers’ over ambulance delays
text:
Queensland's health minister says he has spoken with several families whose loved ones died waiting for an ambulance after sustained media pressure.

Tim Nicholls's compassion was called into question in recent media reports, after he stated he had not personally reached out to those impacted and was waiting for a request for a meeting from the families.

Fronting media today for his first lengthy press conference since the revelations of three deaths of people waiting for ambulances in one weekend, and six since July, he denied dodging reporters.

"I've never not fronted up to the media," Mr Nicholls said. "I've never run away from responsibility."

Family of veteran who died after 18-hour ambulance wait call for answers The deaths of three people waiting for an ambulance in Queensland described as "avoidable".

Mr Nicholls held an 11-minute doorstop press conference on Thursday last week on the deaths and has not faced questions from reporters again until this morning.

He confirmed he is not aware of any further deaths due to ambulance delays or lengthy wait times.

He confirmed he has "spoken with a number of the families [and] next of kin" of those who died and has organised to meet with one of the families.

"Like me, they want to know the answers to what happened," Mr Nicholls said. "I offered [that the] clinical incident review would be made available to them."

When asked whether he should have responded to the deaths differently, Mr Nicholls said he "wakes up every morning and [wonders how he] could do things differently".

Minister 'heartless', opposition leader says

Opposition Leader Steven Miles said reaching out to the families of those who died was "the least" the minister could do.

"It's not just an exercise in showing empathy, although it is that, it is also an opportunity for him to learn precisely what is going on in the community, so that he can address it," Mr Miles said.

Tim Nicholls held a press conference at Queensland parliament last week holding a folding that said "Labor's hospital failures". (ABC News)

He also took aim at Mr Nicholls's short press conference at state parliament last week, during which he held a folder labelled "Labor's hospital crisis".

"To hold an 11-minute press conference, which he tried to turn into a political stunt with that folder, tells you everything you need to know about him; he is heartless, he has no empathy."

Plugging project to deliver 249 new beds

Mr Nicholls spoke with media outside the Princess Alexandra Hospital, to spruik progress on an expansion project to deliver 249 new beds.

It is anticipated construction will be completed by the end of 2027, but it will take months for the beds to slowly come online.

Mr Nicholls said delivering beds is the key to helping fix the health crisis.

"It will be better when those beds that we need are delivered, and that's why we are relentlessly focused on delivering all of those beds, making sure that they are available at the quickest time possible."

title: Minister declares Alice Springs Hospital mould-free despite staff concerns
text:
The Northern Territory health minister says Alice Springs Hospital is free of mould, despite allegations from a health workers' union that staff have reported mould for years.

Steve Edgington told reporters on Monday that recent testing at the hospital had returned negative results.

"The testing that we have conducted on the alleged mould in Alice Springs has come back negative," he said.

" So there was no mould in Alice Springs. "

However, NT Health has since clarified that its investigation covered "identified areas" of the hospital.

Questions remain about where and how testing was conducted, and whether it covered all areas where staff previously reported mould.

Steve Edgington says testing for mould at Alice Springs Hospital returned negative results. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

When asked whether longstanding staff complaints were inaccurate, Mr Edgington maintained that testing had identified no mould.

He said the findings had been communicated to hospital staff through management, but he was unaware of their response.

Years of complaints

In October, the Health Services Union (HSU) raised concerns about what it described as widespread mould at Alice Springs Hospital, alleging workers had repeatedly reported the problem for years.

HSU SA/NT branch secretary Billy Elrick identified the hospital's podiatry treatment room as a particular concern because it treats vulnerable patients, including people who have undergone amputations.

Billy Elrick raised concerns about widespread mould at Alice Springs Hospital in October. (ABC News: Tilda Colling)

At the time, Mr Edgington said he had asked NT Health's chief executive to investigate after becoming aware of the allegations on October 27.

NT Health deputy chief executive of regional services Fiona Renshaw said the investigation was completed on October 28, a day after the minister said he became aware of the allegations.

Ms Renshaw said the results confirmed, "there is no mould growth in the identified areas in Alice Springs Hospital".

She said staff had been informed of the outcome and the department would continue to engage with workers about their concerns.

NT Health has not provided the ABC with a copy of its mould investigation report. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

NT Health did not provide the investigation report to the ABC, nor did it specify which areas were examined, how testing was conducted or whether mould had previously been detected.

The ABC also sought comment from the union about whether staff accepted the findings and whether it had photographic or documentary evidence of mould.

The union had not responded by publication.

Darwin mould problem remains unresolved

Meanwhile, Mr Edgington acknowledged mould remained an ongoing problem at Casuarina Plaza in Darwin, where NT Health services are based.

"It seems to be an ongoing problem with the mould," he said.

"It still hasn't been fully resolved."

Mould remains an ongoing problem at Casuarina Plaza, where NT Health services are based. (Supplied)

The minister said cleaning was continuing while the department searched for alternative premises in Darwin's northern suburbs.

In July, NT Health's chief executive Susan Bowden acknowledged the building had a recurring mould problem, describing the situation as "unacceptable".

The minister said suitable replacement premises had been difficult to find.

title: Inside the great homework debate dividing our teachers, parents and students
text:
Advertisement

Exclusive NationalNSWEducation Inside the great homework debate dividing our teachers, parents and students Christopher Harris November 24, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The reluctance of some NSW public schools to set homework is exacerbating social inequalities as more privileged parents seek out tutoring to address perceived gaps in their children’s education, according to new research. NSW schools have the power to decide whether to enforce homework, with a Department of Education policy document from 2012 stating “research regarding the value of homework is inconclusive”. Other academics have said homework doesn’t improve learning outcomes in primary school. Delia Suteja Yeboah sets her 8-year-old daughter Myla extra maths work at home. Louise Kennerley But those claims are challenged in a new paper from academics at Western Sydney University and UTS, which says homework helps build study routines and students’ ability to read and perform mathematical tasks quickly and easily. The authors said part of the problem with the hundreds of studies on homework is that its benefits were cumulative, often over years, so it was difficult to capture in academic research.

Advertisement

It is also difficult to separate academic outcomes associated with homework from other variables, such as a classroom teacher’s influence on a student. Related Article Education Why parents are calling for the return of primary school homework “Ensuring that students revise classwork and reinforce their conceptual understanding has compounding effects. This is also the case with the much-maligned rote learning,” the research said. “On balance, with certain caveats, the weight of research indicates that homework is beneficial.” The homework findings were part of a bigger research endeavour, Schooling, Parenting and Ethnicity: Asian Migration and Australian Education project, conducted by researchers across Western Sydney University and UTS as part of a three-year project.

Advertisement

It was prompted by a need to better understand the growing impact of Asian migrant families on Australian schooling. Lead researcher from Western Sydney University, Professor Megan Watkins, said repeated practice, particularly in the early years of school, helped students master what they had learnt, reducing cognitive load and allowing students to give greater attention to higher-order thinking. “Many parents were quite upset their children didn’t get more homework,” she said. A major study has challenged widely held beliefs about the benefits of homework. Dominic Lorrimer Researchers interviewed dozens of teachers, students and parents about attitudes at six primary schools across Sydney at varying levels of social disadvantage and ethnic backgrounds. Homework is just one prong of the major study, which also probed Asian parents’ attitudes towards Australian schooling as well as the impact of coaching centres and tutoring culture.

Advertisement

One teacher told the researchers: “Our kids are so bombarded with tutoring that they don’t need the homework.” But parents had a different view, enrolling their children in tutoring because of insufficient homework in schools. The sample size of 500 parents revealed 20 per cent of respondents of an Indian or Chinese background spent 60 minutes or more on homework each night, compared to less than 2 per cent of the respondents from an Anglo background. However, many teachers could see the benefits of homework despite the push against it. “[They] thrive on this extra homework, especially the Chinese students,” one teacher said. Another teacher also favourably viewed homework, but her principal thought it was of zero importance.

Advertisement

Related Article Sorry, your browser doesn't support embedded videos. Exclusive

Education Years ago, a primary school banned homework. Now it’s changed its mind While some parents who could afford it sent their child to tutoring, one mother took it on herself to develop extra school work, visiting education bookstores regularly and planning her own homework based on the term’s classroom activities. Students surveyed described their homework as “minimal and optional”; some said it was “too easy”. Of those who were not given homework, many felt they should have been. The research ultimately found a case for homework. “Clearly, when schools don’t provide homework, many parents and students look for alternatives, such as academic tutoring, further exacerbating inequalities within school communities,” it said.

Advertisement

A NSW Department of Education spokesperson said the homework policy referenced by the academics was outdated and current guidelines did not refer to “inconclusive” research. “Setting homework is a common expectation in NSW public schools,” the spokesman said. “Each school is required to develop homework guidelines that outline their approach and are tailored to the needs of their students.” Delia Suteja Yeboah came to Australia from Indonesia in the 1990s where she learnt the discipline of doing homework every day from kindergarten. “Whether you are rich, you are poor, you go to public school, private school, you are taught in the same similar discipline,” she said.

Advertisement

Her daughter Myla, 8, receives homework each week including a spelling list of 30 words. She adds a maths questionnaire every morning for her daughter to complete and quizzes her when they’re out of the house. Recently, at a sushi restaurant, she quizzed Myla on the cost of the bill based on how many plates they had consumed. “Now I understand as a parent that I need to be able to make it fun and make it practical,” she said. “When I was in Indonesia, the study was way harder.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. title: NSW leads in voluntary assisted dying but telehealth barriers persist
text:
Advertisement

NationalNSWEuthanasia NSW leads in voluntary assisted dying but telehealth barriers persist Jack Gramenz November 24, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. More people chose to end their lives in NSW under the state’s voluntary assisted dying (VAD) program than any other jurisdiction, but access for regional and rural applicants remains limited by an effective ban on telehealth. In the 12 months to the end of June this year, 1419 people died in NSW after administration of a voluntary assisted dying substance, an average of nearly four people per day and an increase of 38 per cent in the second full year of the state’s assisted dying program. NSW was the last state to introduce voluntary assisted dying. NSW MPs voting during the successful passage of the Voluntary Assisted Dying Bill in 2021. Dean Lewins / AAP The figures are contained in the NSW Voluntary Assisted Dying Board’s annual report, released on Monday. Advocacy group Go Gentle’s chief executive Linda Swan said it was expected NSW would have the most people dying in this way, as it has the highest population.

Advertisement

“Even so, VAD deaths account for a tiny proportion of all deaths in the state,” Swan said. Go Gentle chief executive Dr Linda Swan says forcing seriously unwell people to travel long distances for assessments is cruel and unnecessary. James Brickwood In Queensland, 1082 people died during the same reporting period, a slightly larger proportion of that state’s population. Victoria reported 780 deaths among people issued a permit, but 268 of those died without being administered a voluntary assisted dying substance. WA recorded 541 deaths. The ACT’s program began operating last year and the Northern Territory’s will begin in 2028.

Advertisement

Services in NSW are also well-funded in comparison to other jurisdictions and ensure people have access to multiple end-of-life options, Swan said. Related Article Vale Witty and warm, James Valentine lifted the spirits of a city “There is also a growing awareness of the VAD option, partially as a result of several recent high profile VAD deaths – James Valentine and Lex Marinos,” Swan said. But the chief executive of Right To Life UK said the NSW figures were deeply alarming. Alisdair Hungerford-Morgan urged against any expansion, calling for a review of the state’s system “including whether claimed safeguards in current legislation are protecting vulnerable people in practice”.

Advertisement

The state’s VAD board is an independent oversight body which decides whether people applying for access to voluntary assisted dying can access the program, among other functions. Advocates spread messages of support behind NSW Parliament during the campaign to legalise voluntary assisted dying. Nick Moir The report notes equity of access regardless of location is a key principle of the state’s laws and more than two-thirds of the 2875 initial assessments for access in the reporting period were for people outside the Greater Sydney area. Regional areas generally have older populations than major cities. Board chair Jenni Millbank said the board is an advocate for changing federal laws to remove “restrictions on the use of carriage services for steps in the voluntary assisted dying process that would otherwise be lawful and clinically appropriate to occur via audiovisual communication such as telehealth”. Swan said people looking to access telehealth were seriously unwell and in no condition to travel long distances for assessments.

Advertisement

“Expecting them to do so when an alternative exists in the form of telehealth is cruel and unnecessary. “This is about putting the needs of dying people first, rather than forcing them to navigate unnecessary barriers at the end of their lives,” Swan said. Because of a Federal Court ruling in 2023 that voluntary assisted dying is considered suicide, laws preventing the use of a carriage service (such as voice or video calls and emails) to incite or provide information about suicide have prevented doctors providing telehealth consults on euthanasia. It has also led to prolonged suffering for some, due to delays in accessing substances in some states where scripts had to be sent by mail rather than electronically. Health ministers from Victoria, South Australia, Tasmania, Western Australia and the ACT wrote to federal Health Minister Mark Butler and Attorney-General Michelle Rowland in October urging the laws be amended to allow for patients to be assessed for euthanasia via telehealth. “For many people in our states and territories, access to VAD is restricted by where they live,” the ministers wrote.

Advertisement

“This is an issue of equity.” Attorney-General Michelle Rowland speaking at Labor’s national conference in July. Dominic Lorrimer But NSW and Queensland did not join the call. Health Minister Ryan Park said changing the law was a federal responsibility but NSW supports eligible patients to access the scheme in all parts of the state. “The report shows voluntary assisted dying is meeting the needs of those who require it, and that its systems and processes are working effectively,” Park said.

Advertisement

“Ensuring safe and equitable access for all eligible people underpins the approach to voluntary assisted dying in NSW.” Labor Party members voted in July to amend the criminal code to allow telehealth assessments but also guaranteed MPs a conscience vote on the issue if it goes to parliament. Rowland cited concerns that changes could facilitate elder abuse and said it was “fundamentally a health policy issue”. Get alerts on breaking news as it happens. title: RBA could start rate cuts by June as Chalmers flags public service savings
text:

PoliticsFederalAustralian economy RBA could start rate cuts by June as Chalmers flags public service savings Shane Wright and Paul Sakkal Updated November 24, 2026 — 7:19pm ,first published 5:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The Reserve Bank could be forced into cutting interest rates by the middle of next year to salvage the jobs market, one of the nation’s biggest lenders has predicted, while Chalmers flags savings in the public service to rein in government spending. As Opposition Leader Angus Taylor declared the Coalition could return to power next year because the government had mismanaged the economy, the ANZ became the first major commercial bank to predict the RBA would have to reverse its aggressive monetary policy stance due to the deteriorating economic outlook. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Treasurer Dr Jim Chalmers and Minister for Small Business, Minister for International Development, and Minister for Multicultural Affairs Dr Anne Aly Alex Ellinghausen On Tuesday, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese talked up Labor’s preparation for the next election in a caucus meeting, while the Liberal leader projected optimism to beat a government that is “on the rocks” and could head to the polls next year. “Make no mistake about it, colleagues: we can win the next election,” Taylor told a partyroom meeting. The next election is not due until May 2028 and the prime minister is not expected to call an early poll.

Advertisement

On Monday, Treasurer Jim Chalmers said his upcoming mid-year budget update would reveal a grim economic outlook with inflation likely to remain elevated until the second half of next year, unemployment above 5 per cent and larger budget deficits from 2027-28. He said a series of factors, including the spike in oil prices, the AI construction boom and higher interest rates were all weighing on the economy, which will be smaller than forecast in the May budget. Chalmers told ABC’s 7.30 on Tuesday that the government was looking for savings in the “efficiency of the public service”. Two weeks ago, this masthead reported Labor would examine public service cuts as well as winding back generous subsidies for batteries and EVs, which Chalmers also appeared to confirm. “Obviously, we’ll have to look at some of the programs which have been quite successful to make sure that they’re sustainable,” he said. “We’ll have to look at the efficiency of the public service, and in other areas.”

Advertisement

Figures to be released on Wednesday are expected to show inflation in October jumping from 4.3 per cent to almost 5 per cent because of last month’s large jump in oil prices. Related Article Federal budget ‘No use pretending otherwise’: Chalmers warns of tough year ahead as jobless and inflation forecasts worsen ANZ’s head of Australian economics, Adam Boyton, said it was clear the jobs market was weakening more than expected. He said a higher unemployment rate plus the growing evidence of a slowdown across the property market, including signs that advertised rents are starting to fall, meant the RBA would likely start considering a rate cut by June. The Reserve on a 6-3 vote earlier this month lifted the cash rate to an 18-year high of 4.85 per cent. “We are bringing forward our timing for the first RBA rate cut to June 2027. We then expect a follow-up cut in August, taking the cash rate to 4.35 per cent. A further easing in early 2028 will bring the cash rate to 4.1 per cent,” he said.

Advertisement

A rate cut in June, after an increase in November, would be one of the shortest turnarounds in monetary policy this century. The smallest gap was five months between December 2001, when the RBA cut interest rates, and May the following year when it started to lift borrowing costs. When the Reserve raised rates this month, it expected oil prices to average almost $US110 a barrel to December and then ease to $US95 a barrel. But in a positive development for the global and domestic economy, oil has dropped by almost 24 per cent since late October. It fell below $US89 a barrel on Tuesday. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has told colleagues they can win the next federal election. Dominic Lorrimer That is already feeding into petrol prices, with the average across the nation’s major capital cities falling from $2.40 a litre in late October to a two-month low of $2.05 a litre last week.

Advertisement

Chalmers has said in a bid to further reduce inflation pressures his budget update will include “budget-sized” savings, suggesting reductions worth billions of dollars. Pressure to curb inflation has pushed Labor away from one-off subsidies, such as electricity rebates, toward more targeted cost-of-living relief. Reprising its 2025 election playbook, and aiming to capitalise on a remaining area of strength against the Coalition as its overall polling position fades, Labor is planning to lean into its healthcare agenda next year. Related Article Opinion

Federal budget Tasmania’s economy is going south, and it will hit the hip pockets of every Australian Shane Wright Senior economics correspondent Following Monday’s freeze of the $25 medicine co-payment, upcoming announcements are expected on lower specialist fees, boosted regional bulk-billing, and expanded roles for pharmacists and allied health workers.

Advertisement

“We’ve still got a big lead on the Coalition in health, so we will lean in next year,” one senior source said. In lifting interest rates, the Reserve Bank has noted the impact of federal and state government spending adding to demand across the economy which has helped fuel the nation’s inflationary pressures. Analysis released by S&P Global on Tuesday said state government spending and debt would continue to grow. By 2030, state debt is now expected to reach $980 billion, up almost a third from $739 billion today. That surge in debt will push up the share of state budgets used to cover interest repayments. Almost 10 per cent of Victoria’s budget will be spent on interest by the end of the decade, with every other state bar WA spending at least 6 per cent. Treasurer Jim Chalmers during question time on Tuesday November 24. Dominic Lorrimer

Advertisement

The ramp-up in state spending is not being driven by NSW or Victoria where expenditure on major projects is expected to ease over coming years. S&P noted that states like South Australia and Queensland – under pressure over the Brisbane Olympics – are “enthusiastically” opening their purse strings. On Tuesday, the Tasmanian government revealed the expected cost of its planned football stadium had increased by $100 million over the past 12 months to $1.23 billion. It had originally been expected to cost $715 million. S&P Global lead analyst Martin Foo said the states were under growing financial pressure. “Australian state budgets are already stretched. In 2027, housing prices and property-related tax revenue could fall even further, while swelling interest costs will heap on more pressure,” he said.

Advertisement

“With collective debt heading towards $1 trillion by 2031, debt-servicing costs will steadily crowd out spending on public services and infrastructure.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

title: Why Langer’s ball tampering spray didn’t make it into Amazon documentary

Amazon cameras were kept away from Justin Langer’s passionate rebuke of the Australian team for toying with the idea of using red frog lollies to illegally shine the ball in their first Test match after the Sandpapergate scandal. Sources with knowledge of the 2018 tour of the UAE, where Australia played two Tests against Pakistan, have confirmed recollections published by broadcaster Gerard Whateley that there was a discussion about using sugar-based sweets to keep the ball shiny in the first Test of the series in Dubai. Justin Langer addresses the media in the UAE in 2018. Getty Images The lollies of choice were red frogs, used typically to help with players’ sugar levels in hot conditions, but at the time forbidden from being taken onto the field because of the team’s hyper sensitivity to bad optics after the South Africa tour earlier in 2018. The use of mints or other sugar-based sweets as an adjunct to saliva had been a common practice in cricket for decades, despite being outlawed as an artificial substance being used on the ball. Saliva was banned outright from being used on the ball amid the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 and players are now restricted to using perspiration only.

Advertisement

Langer makes a point to players in the UAE eight years ago. Getty Images The Amazon documentary series known as The Test has become a recurring part of the national team’s story over the past eight years, and a fourth season is currently being filmed. It was conceived partly to allow access to a dressing room that had previously been a closed shop, and partly to showcase the team’s new direction. But its rules of engagement include the team always having the option of having veto over what is recorded or ultimately broadcast. Countless confidential team discussions have been left on the cutting room floor or not recorded, and a source told this masthead that Langer’s rebuttal of ball tampering was one of them. Loading This masthead has also confirmed that bowlers Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc, Pat Cummins and Nathan Lyon jointly indicated they were not prepared to take responsibility for the ball tampering plot because they felt that David Warner was the architect.

Advertisement

Whateley quoted one member of the quartet as saying: “F---k Davey, we are not going down for that guy.” A source close to the bowlers told this masthead on condition of anonymity that the accuracy of the quote may be disputed, but the overall sentiment is right. The relational chasm between Warner and the bowlers has never quite healed since, and has only grown wider lately. Warner declined to comment when approached by this masthead. Australia in the field during the Dubai Test in 2018. Ryan Pierse/Getty Images Langer’s infuriated response to the floating of ideas about artificially altering the condition of the ball is a reminder that it took Australian cricket a while to reconfigure itself after the sandpaper episode.

Advertisement

Before the recent South Africa Test series, Travis Head told this masthead that he had similarly stamped out discussions about ball tampering in the South Australian dressing room. Head made his Test debut for Australia in the UAE Test match where the subject came up. “I made a pretty strong stand at that point, and I was captain at the time, that they weren’t going to be in the dressing room if that’s the case, if that’s what [they want to do],” Head said last month. “I didn’t care what other teams did. I didn’t care if we were facing it. “I just knew what a couple of close friends had gone through, and knew what the [Australian] team had gone through, and the flow-on effect of that. I don’t care if we’re bottom of the table, as long as we play the game the right way. That was my opinion, and still is my opinion.” Editor's pick Updated

Ball tampering ‘We all knew’: Bancroft claims entire Australian team was aware sandpaper use in South Africa Head also reiterated something that Cricket Australia concluded last week - the team’s improved sense of perspective about playing the game in the right way has been largely driven by skipper Cummins.

Advertisement

“It’s driven from Pat. Pat’s always said it’s a game, and it’s not do or die,” Head said. “If South Africa play really, really well, and we lose 3-0, that’s OK; it’s not the end of the world. We’ll wake up tomorrow. I think that then brings in, I guess, that freer side of yourself to go out and express yourself. “We’ve seen other teams around the world hold on to certain things or think it’s the most important thing they’re ever going to do, and sometimes you can play on that. You can see that they get tense and feel pressure, and you never play better when you’re tense and feel pressured.” Related Article Australian cricket Paine the peacemaker: Ex-skipper looms as key figure in Sandpapergate talks CA declined to comment on Whateley’s investigation, but the governing body is working to finalise terms of reference for the “truth forum” to be conducted to allow members of the 2018 South African tour party to share their often conflicting recollections. “It meant a lot to speak with David and Todd on Friday. Being Australian captain carries with it an awesome responsibility,” Cummins said last week after meeting with chair David Boon and chief executive Todd Greenberg.

title: How Bluey exported Brisbane to viewers who didn’t think its setting was real
text:

NationalQueenslandCityChats How Bluey exported Brisbane to viewers who didn’t think its setting was real Nick Dent , Dominique Tassell and Neesha Sinnya November 24, 2026 — 7:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items.
