Welcome to CityChats, where Brisbane Times meets our city’s most interesting characters on its most iconic form of transport. This week, we meet Ludo Studio co-founder Daley Pearson, who helped give the world Bluey, is executive producer of The Bluey Movie, and has just directed his first live action movie, Allen. We’re waiting for our CityCat when the Bluey “CityDog” comes by, going in the other direction. Daley Pearson can’t help but notice its paintwork is starting to look a bit faded. We get on board a regular ferry and start the interview in the hot morning sun. Daley Pearson has co-directed feature film Allen. Netflix Here we are on a CityCat. In a way, it’s a shame it’s not a CityDog. We can imagine.

Advertisement

It must be odd for you that this thing [Bluey] that you helped kick off 10 years ago is now everywhere, to the extent that it’s in shops, it’s on kids’ backpacks, and it’s on boats in Brisbane. It’s hard to comprehend sometimes. It’s quite nice being in Brisbane because you feel like you’re in a little protected bubble in some ways, that the people who’ve mostly heard about it are your cousins and your uncles ... I remember going to New York with the team to see [the giant Bluey in the] Macy’s Parade … it felt a bit surreal. Hearing American families talk about it in front of you on the subway, that was very bizarre. You’ve done more with Ludo, arguably, to promote Brisbane to the world – Oh, that’s a nice thing.

Advertisement

– than the tourism boards. Arguably. Related Article CityChats Ranger Stacey on her biggest animal mishap: ‘Luckily it was non-venomous’ Arguably. I didn’t say that! To me, Bluey has done such a fantastic job of conveying what’s lovely about this city. Was that something you felt should be part of the show’s DNA? I think Joe [Brumm] did – Joe’s the creator of Bluey. It was totally done under one roof, and we built the studio for it. [It was] just naturally Brisbane, because everyone was from there. The designers drew from the world around them. You’d see them in the corner of the office, these brilliant artists colour-roughing or sketching the afternoon pink sun or the morning in Brisbane, or CityCats … it’s just all very natural.

Advertisement

And do people from other countries realise that the show actually does convey what life is like in Brisbane? I remember one of the very early first reviews was in The New York Times, and it said the show was set on a tropical island. It didn’t mention Australia or Brisbane. But it also was kind of right: we are tropical, we are an island! So they were halfway there, but they were sort of talking about it as if it was Oz, you know, an imaginary, made-up place ... I remember laughing at that one. Related Article Cinema Life after Bluey: What the team behind the world’s biggest show did next One of the things people love about Bluey is that it has helped them connect with their children, and also with their own childhoods, [even] people who have suffered childhood pain. And in a way, your new Netflix film, Allen, is also about those things. It’s about a character who’s had this incredible childhood, and then he lost something – it’s a little alien, which is ridiculous – and he spent his whole life in arrested development trying to get it back. There’s definitely a metaphor there.

Advertisement

I’ve had my own stuff – everyone’s had something. I had a brother who passed away, and he was brilliant, he was my best friend, and he is my best friend. But, you know, people who have had divorce, or your dog runs away – it doesn’t have to be big, it could be small – whatever that thing that pops you out of childhood is, you want to keep trying to get it back, at the expense of maybe the future. But it’s really just a giddy film, hopefully a funny film, about a guy who grew up in Coolum Beach, which I did, who lost a little alien friend. Allen has some of the wonderful hallmarks of Spielberg films. The music, the special effects, the alien that you’ve created. The ferry makes a sudden jolt. These have quite a kick in them, these CityCats. [CityCat crew member: “We got some new engines recently!”]

Advertisement

Yeah, I used to take these to Sizzler at Toowong, and these are definitely a little bit faster. Anyway, we tried not to make it an imitation of Spielberg or E.T., even though it’s so hard not to, ’cos it is what it is. But we tried to tell a story that was using the stuff that we couldn’t let go of – all this nostalgic stuff – using that to tell a new story about trying to let go of it. What would you say is Brisbane’s problem? It doesn’t have many. I remember on Mother’s Day, the city was like blocked, it was like a Die Hard movie, it was bumper to bumper, nobody could get anywhere. And I was like, ‘I wonder how this will be for the Olympics if Mother’s Day brings us all to a halt’. And do you have a controversial Brisbane opinion?

Advertisement

I feel like we should have kept our Sizzler open. Allen is streaming on Netflix. The Bluey Movie opens on August 6. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. Sign up for our Morning Edition newsletter.

title: The changes to expect at your child’s school – no matter who wins the election
text:
Advertisement

PoliticsVictoriaEducation The changes to expect at your child’s school – no matter who wins the election Alex Crowe November 24, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Building more select-entry schools and scrapping payroll tax are among the changes Victorians could see in education after the state election. While both major parties are committed to explicit teaching and improving literacy and numeracy results, other policies set them apart. Victoria Petrevska and Nikola Breshovski, pictured with their children, are watching what the parties are promising for bilingual education. Wayne Taylor The Liberal/National coalition has announced a string of changes that will impact students and schools, including a curriculum review, while Labor has focused primarily on expanding existing programs and upgrading schools. Minor parties have also pitched major changes, with the Greens promising to scrap voluntary fees in public schools and One Nation proposing a ban on the burqa and niqab on campuses.

Advertisement

With such a wide suite of promises, we asked three education experts to weigh in on what the parties were offering to win your vote. Monash University Dean of Education Mary Ryan, University of Melbourne Professor in Educational Leadership Pasi Sahlberg and Deakin University PhD candidate Tom Mahoney give their verdict. The Coalition Scrap the payroll tax High-fee private schools have claimed annual fee increases, as high as 15.1 per cent, are a consequence of Labor’s decision to strip them of their long-held payroll tax exemption in 2024.

Advertisement

The tax, which was projected to deliver an estimated $101.8 million to the state budget last year, applies to schools with annual fees of $16,397 or more and is due to continue until January 1, 2029. But the Coalition has promised to free all schools of the tax burden, under the assumption private schools will pass on the savings to parents. Mahoney said fewer than 10 per cent of private schools, all high-fee, would benefit from this policy, with savings unlikely to flow through to parents. “There’s only 60 non-government schools out of about 700 that are currently paying the payroll tax, and those schools are the ones charging the highest fees to parents,” he said.

Advertisement

Mahoney said non-government schools had been raising fees year-on-year well before the payroll tax was introduced and there was no evidence to suggest they’d raise them less if it were scrapped. “There are plenty of other ways that I would say non-government schools can reduce their fees, such as reducing their building projects,” he said. Sahlberg said scrapping the schools payroll tax was “an ineffective promise” and he’d much rather see the Coalition commit to fully fund all public schools by 2030. “Surely, fixing that should come first.” Literacy and Numeracy Guarantee

Advertisement

One in three Australian students needed additional support to meet national numeracy and literacy benchmarks in NAPLAN for three consecutive years, while the latest round of international testing reported Australia’s worst-ever result. While Victorian students scored higher than the national average across all NAPLAN disciplines for a second consecutive year and outperformed students in all other states in writing and numeracy, efforts to boost proficiency, including the rollout of explicit teaching, have yet to yield significant improvements. The Coalition plans to fix that by setting a target to improve results by 15 per cent over the next decade and a long-term goal of 90 per cent proficiency across literacy and numeracy. To achieve this, they’ve promised professional learning for teachers and a curriculum review to “better prepare students for life while reducing workload on teachers”.

Advertisement

Monash University Dean of Education Mary Ryan. Ryan said setting targets was useful, but the policy lacked detail and focused on the overall result, rather than lifting proficiency among children who performed poorly on NAPLAN – including those from remote and low-socioeconomic communities. “For a start, we probably need to know what the target applies to: is it year level? Is it overall? “What are we going to do to lift those particular cohorts? Because if we lift those cohorts, that will make a huge difference,” she said. Ryan said it was also unclear how the Coalition would review the curriculum while reducing teacher workloads.

Advertisement

“A review of the curriculum is going to be a lot of work for teachers,” she said. Build three new select-entry high schools and transition six existing public schools to select or partial select-entry Victoria currently has four select-entry schools, and competition for places has become so fierce there are more than six applications for every spot offered. The Coalition wants to buy land in Melbourne’s three fastest-growing regions – the west, north and outer south-east – for three new select-entry schools. Ryan said the problem with select-entry schools was the impact on non-selective schools of plucking out their brightest students.

Advertisement

“It changes the whole demographic of those schools ... it changes the resourcing; it sometimes changes the expectations [of students],” she said. Sahlberg said research showed selective schools tended to attract students from more advantaged backgrounds. “So, rather than making [the] Victorian education system fairer, this could actually make the gaps between public schools even wider,” he said. “If we have $150 million extra public dollars to invest in education, I would put that into schools serving Victoria’s most disadvantaged communities, where better teaching, additional support and stronger learning opportunities could benefit many more children. That would be a much better investment in our state’s future.” Shadow education minister Brad Rowswell introduced Successful School Starters at The Age education summit. Turbo360

Advertisement

Occupational health and speech pathologists to identify neurodiverse students As diagnoses of neurodivergent conditions in Australia have soared in the past decade, so has the number of children in classrooms with complex learning needs. If the Coalition wins, Victorian children will be observed in their first year of schooling for signs of autism or ADHD to fast-track early interventions. Mahoney said teachers were already proficient at identifying students with additional needs. He said the real issue was lack of resources to support students who had received a diagnosis.

Advertisement

Deakin University education expert Tom Mahoney. “It’s a bit short-sighted in that it’s assuming that the diagnosis is what is needed to be able to support these students,” Mahoney said. Establish 10 new technical colleges statewide Providing alternative pathways for students who don’t want to attend university has been a focus for both major parties. Under the Coalition’s plan, about 5000 students would enrol in industry training focused on construction and engineering in 10 specialised colleges while completing their VCE at a cost of $222 million over eight years.

Advertisement

Ryan said providing alternative pathways for students was important, but she was concerned it could limit the options for students if they changed their mind on pursuing a trade. “Some of the trades now, they need to be learning skills that are similar to a mechanical engineering degree.” Ryan said Australia was also seeing fewer students going into trades, and while this seemed to be a case of “build it, and they will come”, she wasn’t convinced. Student and teacher leadership councils The Coalition has promised to give students and teachers a direct pathway to the education minister by establishing student and teacher councils in every electorate.

Advertisement

Local MPs would chair the councils with the aim of having classroom experiences heard by decision makers. Labor Free kinder Labor began providing free kinder for three- and four-year-olds statewide from 2023, after a staged rollout starting in regional Victoria in 2020. Under its plan, free kindergarten for four-year-olds would double from the current 15 hours a week to 30 hours statewide by 2036, while three-year-old kinder would scale up to 15 hours a week by 2029.

Advertisement

Education Minister Gabrielle Williams. Justin McManus While vowing free kinder is here to stay, the Coalition has pledged to undertake a review of the early learning sector to improve accessibility and quality, “and examine how Labor’s regulatory changes have affected childcare”. Free kinder is one of several existing policies Labor has promised to expand, including broadening its free dental check-ups in schools program to include kinders. School upgrades Since being in power, Labor has prioritised new school builds, with 121 new public schools opened since 2017.

Advertisement

As part of its election promises, Labor has pledged $1.17 billion to upgrade 228 public schools and $500 million to upgrade independent schools. New selective and independent schools Building on the John Monash Science School model, Labor has promised to establish more specialist selective schools, starting with a new maths and science school in Melbourne’s north. A re-elected Labor government would invest $135 million to establish the public school for up to 650 students from years 9 to 12 at La Trobe University’s Bundoora campus. It will also spend $15 million to build Victoria’s first Sikh school, teaching the curriculum alongside Sikh religious, cultural and language traditions.

Advertisement

Two new TAFE campuses The building of two new TAFE campuses in Melbourne’s outer north and west is on the agenda with further upgrades of campuses in Bendigo, Wonthaggi and Dandenong, for a combined $170 million. Smart glasses Labor has promised to expand the ban on mobile devices in all schools to include a ban on smart glasses and wearable devices. Languages

Advertisement

One new initiative is a $43 million pledge to increase the languages available to students in VCE, through the Victorian School of Languages (VSL). VSL currently offers 17 VCE languages through remote learning. Labor would expand that to all 44 modern VCE languages from 2028. Macedonian-Australian Victoria Petrevska said the language program’s expansion would mean she could send her son to any nearby secondary school, confident he could continue his language studies. Petrevska said her son was currently building foundation language skills at the Macedonian bilingual primary school in Lalor. “We’re really thankful for any kind of program that helps bilingual students access bilingual education,” Petrevska said.

Advertisement

University of Melbourne professor Pasi Sahlberg. Nine Mahoney said his concern with the policy was that it assumed there was high enough demand for the work required to implement it. Asked to give an overall assessment on Labor’s track record on education, Sahlberg said they deserved credit for some positive developments in Victorian schools. He highlighted improvements in foundation literacy, progress in keeping students engaged in secondary education and Victoria achieving the country’s strongest overall NAPLAN results. “My concern is that, despite these achievements, Labor’s approach to education remains rather conservative, focusing more on improving schools as we have known them than reinventing schooling for a rapidly changing world,” he said.

Advertisement

“Good NAPLAN results bring some political comfort for sure, but they don’t tell us everything about the quality of education. And when enrolments in non-government schools are growing faster than those in public schools, we should be asking why more families are looking elsewhere for their children’s education.” Sahlberg said the most difficult question for Labor was on funding. “After more than a decade in government, why hasn’t Labor made free public education by fully funding every Victorian public school by 2030 its central election promise?” One Nation Warren Pickering’s team is focusing on streamlining the curriculum and lifting standards and discipline.

Advertisement

In addition to replacing the “overcrowded curriculum”, One Nation would allow schools greater flexibility to offer programs that reflect their community, such as agriculture, trades, sport, music, technology or the arts. The party has vowed to make it easier for parents and communities to establish new independent, specialist and alternative schools. It would also introduce a voucher system that would give funding directly to parents for them to spend on the school of their choice. Asked to summarise, Sahlberg said One Nation’s policy to give schools more flexibility to offer programs that reflect local needs and its policy to expand trade schools were “sensible”. “But overall, I find their education agenda disappointing,” he said.

Advertisement

“There is practically nothing here to fix the chronic underfunding of public schools, tackle growing inequalities in educational outcomes, or prepare young people for a world shaped by artificial intelligence, changing work and an increasingly unstable planet.” One Nation’s Victorian leader Warren Pickering. Luis Enrique Ascui Sahlberg said their promises would introduce more political control over schools. “I am particularly concerned about their proposals for school vouchers and expanding independent and alternative schools,” he said. “Instead of building a stronger and fairer public education system, we risk creating more competition and division between schools.”

Advertisement

Ryan said voucher systems were problematic because families don’t have equal access to the school of their choice. “Vouchers are not going to work for every family, and schools might then be competing for students rather than lifting outcomes for all students and meeting the needs of communities.” She said a voucher system would also be very difficult to implement. Ryan said banning burqas and niqabs in schools was potentially contravening equal opportunity, human rights and discrimination legislation. “For me, that raises serious educational, ethical, and legal concerns,” she said.

Advertisement

Ryan said there was no evidence that religious dress was a barrier to integration. “Those two particular issues really stand out as problematic, and it would be very unlikely that they could be implemented in Australia,” she said. Greens leader Ellen Sandell. AAP The Greens The minor party isn’t short on ideas for our public education system, publishing 30 education “principles”, and 66 “aims” under eight categories, including improved conditions for educators and funding and infrastructure.

Advertisement

Mahoney said Ellen Sandell’s team showed a strong commitment to fully funding public schools, which he saw as a top priority. However, he said making school completely free by banning parent contributions was flawed. “Schools rely on parent contributions and fundraising to get the basics, and it shouldn’t be that way, but we can’t ignore the reality that it is,” he said. Mahoney said he also had a problem with the Greens’ push to mandate domestic, family and sexual violence education for students in years 10 to 12. “[It] disregards what’s already done through the Respectful Relationships curriculum,” he said.

Advertisement

title: Brooke’s research aimed to help women. So why did some people wish her dead?
text:
Advertisement

LifestyleHealth & wellnessBreast cancer Brooke’s research aimed to help women. So why did some people wish her dead? Sarah Berry November 24, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Dr Brooke Nickel’s work in cancer communication is personal. The Canadian-born researcher was four years old when her mother died of breast cancer. So when breast density screening notifications began in the United States and Australia in 2009, Nickel was intrigued. At the time, her research was focused on how to reduce the harms of overdiagnosis and overtreatment in cancer. University of Sydney researcher Dr Brooke Nickel wanted to help women. She didn’t expect the backlash. Sam Mooy “I thought it was fascinating from a public health perspective, from a cancer perspective and from a women’s health perspective,” recalls Nickel, a senior research fellow in the School of Public Health at the University of Sydney.

Advertisement

And, she adds, “It definitely felt close to my heart.” The right to know The push for notifications arose from a grassroots campaign spearheaded by American activist Nancy Cappello. Cappello was diagnosed with advanced breast cancer in 2003 when her doctor found a lump in her breast. When she asked why it wasn’t detected in the mammogram she had weeks earlier, Cappello was told that she had dense breast tissue – more fibrous and glandular tissue than fatty tissue – which can mask abnormalities: dense tissue and cancers both show up as white on mammograms. Up to 50 per cent of women have dense breast tissue, which is associated with about a twofold increase in the risk of breast cancer.

Advertisement

Cappello, who died in 2018 of a rare blood cancer related to the chemotherapy and radiation she received for breast cancer, campaigned for women’s right to be notified if they had dense breast tissue, so they could decide whether to get additional screening. Related Article Women's health Four daily habits gynaecologists say transform women’s health in midlife Following the lead of the US, these notifications have become routine in other countries, including in many parts of Australia. This well-intentioned movement became a “hot topic” that was having ripple effects across the globe, yet it lacked evidence as a public health strategy. In a randomised controlled trial published in The BMJ in 2025, Nickel investigated the psychological effect on women who received notifications and whether it prompted them to see their doctor or pursue further scans.

Advertisement

Eight weeks after receiving a notification, women were more anxious, confused and did not feel more informed about what to do. Few intended to have additional screenings, which incur out-of-pocket costs. ‘I hope your children know what it’s like to feel motherless’ If the notifications are not changing behaviour, and are making them feel more anxious and confused, then how are they benefiting women, Nickel wondered. “There is this premise of information is power. But, having an intervention that, from a population perspective, has no evidence of overall benefit for women is a bit concerning.” The findings, and Nickel’s questions about the utility of the notifications, hit a nerve. Amidst targeted phone calls and emails were people wishing her dead.

Advertisement

“I had people telling me that ‘I hope your children know what it’s like to feel motherless’ and things that, you know, really hit home when my mum did die of breast cancer,” she says. “When the backlash comes from those people that you do your work to try and help, it’s a tough pill to swallow.” “When the backlash comes from those people that you do your work to try and help, it’s a tough pill to swallow,” said Nickel. Sam Mooy Notifications not founded on robust evidence Yet in a new study, published in The Lancet Primary Care, Nickel and her colleagues followed up with women over at least one year to see whether their initial worry and behaviour changed.

Advertisement

It didn’t. Women who received notifications remained slightly more anxious than those who didn’t, and compared with the control group (women who also had dense breast tissue but did not receive notifications) were no more likely to see their GP or have supplemental screening. “The assumption that providing this density information will prompt women to do additional screening after a ‘clear’ mammogram is not founded on robust evidence,” says co-author Nehmat Houssami, a professor of Public Health at the University of Sydney and the NBCF Chair in Breast Cancer Prevention. Urging additional screening in healthy women can be beneficial, but is also not without risks. Beyond the expense, there can be false-positive results, which lead to biopsy and unnecessary intervention, Houssami explains. “The trade-off between potential benefit and harms of additional screening is, at a population level, not established,” she says.

Advertisement

“For some women there will be benefit (of earlier detection of breast cancer that was not seen on a dense mammogram). For many more women, there will be no benefit (or they will experience harms, false alarms, costs).” Professor Wendy Ingman leads Adelaide University’s Breast Biology and Cancer Unit, based at The Queen Elizabeth Hospital. She says the breast density notifications are “a really great first step”. “I don’t think anyone would argue that we want to stop there.” Ingman, who is the scientific advisor for the Australian Breast Density Consumer Advisory Council, adds that one driver for the notifications has been enabling women to be part of the decision-making process. “If you don’t notify women they have dense breasts, they have no opportunity to be part of decisions about what’s best for their breast health,” she says, adding that such information may make women more breast aware and more likely to return for their next scheduled mammogram.

Advertisement

One thing everyone agrees on is that women who receive notifications need quality information. Getty Images Finding better ways forward It remains a fraught issue. Breast cancer is the most common cancer among women: they are right to want information, and the counterargument is that if the notifications saved the lives of two women, then they are worth it. “Every woman has the right to know and understand her breast cancer risk through standardised breast density reporting,” said Vicki Durston, Breast Cancer Network Australia’s (BCNA) Director of Policy, Advocacy and Support Services, in a 2025 statement.

Advertisement

BCNA maintains that thousands of Australian women are denied knowledge of their increased breast cancer risk because the notifications are not mandated across the country. Nickel and Houssami would like to see equal attention paid to other breast cancer risks, many of which are modifiable. Breast density is roughly similar in risk to a family history of breast cancer, although it depends on the density level. Other risk factors of equal importance include age, alcohol, post-menopausal obesity and sustained use of HRT. One thing everyone agrees on is that women who receive notifications need quality information. Equitable supplementary imaging is part of this, but it’s also about looking at a woman’s breast cancer risk factors holistically and her individual circumstances, Ingman says.

Advertisement

Houssami agrees: “We need to plan more accessible pathways for women, to make sure that the density notification is not contributing to healthcare disparities in cancer screening.” Finally, Nickel is at pains to point out that she agrees women should have information and choice. But, she says, it should be based on the best possible evidence and there ought to be an accessible pathway for them to follow – one that is focused on modifiable behaviours and subsidised scans if that is what women want. “I think women should be given a chance to make an informed decision based on all the available evidence,” she says. “You have to be allowed to know what options exist and what those downstream benefits could be, but also the potential consequences.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. title: A third-country link allowing Nvidia chips to get to China is under scrutiny
text:
In Brief Singapore says its investigation into Megaspeed is continuing as the US moves to blacklist the AI firm.

Singapore's prime minister says the country won't be used to bypass export controls on advanced AI chips.

Singapore's prime minister says the AI firm at the centre of the Nvidia spy scandal is still being investigated there, as the US government moves to blacklist it over allegations that it moved advanced AI chips to China in breach of American export controls.

Speaking in Canberra on Tuesday, Lawrence Wong rejected suggestions that Singapore had become a weak link in the escalating technology competition between the United States and China, while stressing that his government does not want the city-state used to circumvent US export restrictions.

"We do not want Singapore to be used and abused as a conduit by companies to circumvent America's export controls," Wong said when asked by SBS News about the case.

"What we do is facilitate checks by America to enforce its own laws."

The scandal revolves around an extramarital affair between Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy, who worked at Megaspeed, the Singaporean company suspected of diverting restricted AI chips to China.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Alice Huang was in contact with an officer at a Chinese intelligence agency from 2025 until late in 2026, The New York Times reported, citing people briefed on US intelligence reports.

Wong said Singapore had investigated Megaspeed and Alice Huang after concerns emerged that advanced AI chips may have been routed through the company to Chinese customers.

"We were thorough with Alice Huang. We took her in, we investigated her, but we eventually released her because there was no basis for further prosecution. America understands what we have done," he said.

Megaspeed investigations ongoing

Wong said investigations into Megaspeed remain active, particularly on the US side, as authorities in both countries exchange information.

"We are continuing to have discussions with American authorities where the end-users are, to confirm the verification of various documents," Wong said.

"These investigations into Megaspeed are ongoing on the American side."

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese addressed reporters alongside Wong, reiterating his position that the allegations are "serious".

"Is Australia a party to any of these arrangements? Quite clearly not," he said.

"It's a matter for the company, it's a matter for the United States and it's a matter for Singapore."

READ MORE Donald Trump hails Nvidia's reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang after affair scandal

Megaspeed says it's a "legitimate and lawful business" and that Huang left the company in August 2025.

Wong disputed claims that the case showed weaknesses in Singapore's oversight of sensitive technology exports. He said the chips were never intended for use in Singapore and merely passed through the country's commercial networks.

"The chips were routed through Singapore to other countries," he said. "Obviously we cannot investigate all that's happening in these countries."

He added that Singapore has sought more information from US authorities about the ultimate destinations of the chips and is working closely with Washington to help enforce export-control rules.

"We are also looking at companies that may be using Singapore and exploiting Singapore's position to reroute chips through Singapore to other parts of Southeast Asia or to other countries," Wong said.

"We do not have full information on where all these chips are sent to. They are not sent to Singapore as a final destination, but the US has growing interest in this area of chips coming through Singapore and being transited or rerouted."

Megaspeed blacklisted by US authorities

Earlier on Tuesday, the US commerce department announced plans to blacklist Megaspeed and affiliated companies to block them from buying or selling goods in the United States.

US authorities have been investigating the company since at least 2024 over allegations it helped move restricted Nvidia computer chips into China, bypassing export bans imposed by Washington.

China has been restricted from accessing advanced semiconductor technology since 2022 to slow China's development of cutting-edge artificial intelligence systems.

Megaspeed, which operates data centres and cloud computing infrastructure across Southeast Asia, and China both deny the allegations that Alice Huang is linked to Chinese intelligence.

Jensen Huang and Nvidia's general counsel Tim Teter will be questioned in closed-door interviews with US congressional committees examining the scandal.

Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive 11 days after his resignation following consultations with US government officials.

Neither Wong nor Albanese directly addressed questions about Huang's return during the Canberra press conference.

The two leaders signed an agreement to deepen co-operation on AI.

title: Tech giants set to face major fines: How will the updated online safety bill work?
text:
IN BRIEF The Greens have reached an agreement with Labor on passing digital duty of care legislation.

Labor had to make a deal with the Greens after it became clear the Coalition would not support the bill.

Tech giants could be fined billions of dollars and face lawsuits from people harmed by social media algorithms, and a new regulator will offer people a place to appeal, after a deal was made to pass new online safety standards.

Labor's digital duty of care laws will force online services, including social media, online games and AI chatbots, to take reasonable steps to reduce serious online harm.

The reforms will pass the Senate with support from the Greens after the party negotiated concessions from the government on Tuesday.

Labor forfeited ministerial powers to classify new online harms, and carved out small businesses and religious organisations from the bill after a Senate committee suggested changes on Friday.

The Greens, who hold the balance of power in the upper house, forced the government to amend the laws on Tuesday so people can sue tech companies directly for harm caused, and fine platforms up to 5 per cent of global revenue if they fail to shield users from harm caused by addictive algorithms, or fail to take down harmful content.

For Meta, which runs Facebook and Instagram, that could mean fines in the order of $10 billion. Labor's original proposal had set fines at $109 million.

The rate of hateful conduct found on Facebook by users is rising. Source: SBS News

"Like every other company selling products in Australia, big tech will finally be held responsible for the harm that their products cause. Just like food producers and toy manufacturers," Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young said.

People will also have the choice to turn algorithms on or off and see the content they want to see, she said.

"It's time to dump the doomscroll. For the first time, tech companies will now have to recognise the addictive nature of their platforms and prevent harm from features such as infinite scroll, autoplay and gamification that keep Australians hooked online for hours longer than they want to be.

"The Greens have also secured the establishment of an independent ombudsman to help Australian consumers manage disputes with tech platforms."

US ambassador hits out at new laws after meeting minister

Communications Minister Anika Wells said she met with US ambassador David Brat on Tuesday as part of ongoing "constructive dialogue" with the US government.

"It has been a long-signalled intent of our government that we would pass these laws because online safety is such a priority for us. I think the ambassador and I had a really constructive meeting, really friendly meeting," Wells said.

"I think we would say there are points of difference, and we are riding them out."

READ MORE A third-country link allowing Nvidia chips to get to China is under scrutiny

Following the meeting with Wells, Brat said: "Free speech is the foundation of a free society, and protecting it is a US priority".

He said he had expressed to Wells the Trump administration's "well-known objections" to the legislation, saying "vaguely defined 'harms', backed by penalties of up to 5 per cent of global revenue, will push platforms to censor lawful speech".

"As Australia's largest foreign investor, the US is concerned with regulations that impose disproportionate compliance burdens on American companies relative to competitors."

The US embassy forcefully told the government in September to "withdraw any plans to mandate that platforms algorithmically suppress content based on ambiguous government-defined safety criteria".

What platforms have to do

The laws focus on how digital services are designed and managed, so social media firms will need to assess risks and take action to protect users from harmful or illegal material.

They would also have to protect under-18s from content and features that may be harmful, including pornography, material that encourages eating disorders and features that could cause serious distress.

The bill also gives social media users aged 16 and over a choice to turn off algorithm-recommended feeds and see posts from accounts they follow.

It expands the eSafety Commissioner's powers over apps and websites used to create fake nude images, and shortens the required response time for cyberbullying and abuse complaints from 48 hours to 24.

Professional news and entertainment material are exempt from the new laws.

READ MORE Small businesses spared from online crackdown as crunch time looms for government

A new independent ombudsman will help Australians challenge social media account bans and deal with other issues.

Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman (TIO) Cynthia Gebert said thousands of Australians seek help from the TIO when they're locked out of social media and email accounts.

"It's great that Australians will soon have access to a free, fair and independent dispute resolution scheme when big tech gets things wrong," Gebert said.

"We look forward to working with the government on the development of the external dispute resolution scheme."

Why is the Coalition against the bill?

The bill makes platforms responsible for foreseeable harms linked to their services and gives people stronger ways to seek redress. The Coalition has opposed the laws, warning freedom of speech may be policed or curtailed.

Opposition communications spokesperson Sarah Henderson told reporters on Monday the laws threaten "not only the free speech of Australians, but also the online safety of Australians".

"It is a blank cheque for political censorship because it allows the regulator to basically prohibit any type of serious harm directed towards children," Henderson said.

"We have very strong current laws under the Online Safety Act, including the 17 codes and standards, and the eSafety Commissioner is using those laws right now to prosecute Telegram for refusing or declining to remove pro-terror material," she said.

There was little hope the Coalition would support the changes, with the Opposition instead calling for a crackdown on harmful content via existing laws.

Her party was particularly concerned the bill would allow government ministers and the eSafety Commissioner to mandate what was harmful.

Henderson said she will push for better parental protections online when parliament returns next year.

Meta declined to comment. SBS News has also asked Google and TikTok for comment.

title: Donald Trump hails Nvidia's reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang after affair scandal
text:

Huang resigned as CEO after his affair with a woman thought to be a Chinese spy was made public.

Jensen Huang has been reinstated as president and chief executive of Nvidia, just days after his offer to return to the artificial intelligence giant was rejected.

title: Next FIFA Women's World Cup hosts selected for 2031 and 2035
text:
in brief The US will co-host the 2031 Women's World Cup, while a UK bid led by England was ratified for 2035.

Both editions will expand to 48 teams, with all revenue reinvested into women's football.

The United States will host a FIFA World Cup again in 2031, while England will do so for the first time since 1966 four years later.

Football's global governing body has confirmed the US will lead a regional 2031 Women's World Cup co-hosted with Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica. A UK bid led by England was then ratified for the 2035 edition.

FIFA confirmed on Tuesday that the 2031 games will see an expanded 48-team Women's World Cup, on par with the men's tournament held across the US, Mexico and Canada earlier this year.

The winning bids were waved through by acclamation after FIFA president Gianni Infantino confirmed the joint Americas bid was the "sole candidacy" to host in 2031.

The joint English, Scottish, Northern Irish and Welsh bid was also the only candidacy for 2035.

The winners promised commercially successful tournaments, with the proceeds being reinvested into women's football.

"As of 2031 there will be 48 teams and four hosts," Infantino said.

"This is an incredible growth in just a few years."

US Soccer Federation president Cindy Parlow Cone told FIFA members in a pre-vote presentation at the governing body's Zurich headquarters it would be "the largest women's sporting event in history".

"Which means we have to deliver."

US Soccer reacted to the announcement by saying the awarding of the 2031 tournament gave the country the chance to "build on the momentum" of this year's World Cup as well as the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

The US are the reigning Olympic women's football champions.

Tournament selection a 'landmark moment'

It is not yet known which cities will host matches at the respective tournaments, but most matches in 2031 are likely to take place in the US while England can expect to have the lion's share of venues in 2035.

The US-led 2031 project bid offers FIFA a choice of stadiums in 20 cities: 14 in the US, four in Mexico, San José in Costa Rica and Kingston, Jamaica.

The UK bid proposed 22 stadiums in total, with 16 in England, three in Wales, two in Scotland and one in Northern Ireland, including the iconic Wembley Stadium in London.

Scottish Football Association chief executive Ian Maxwell said the two venues in the country would be the 52,000-seat Hampden Park in Glasgow and Hibernian's 20,000-seat Easter Road home in Edinburgh.

The Matildas experienced widespread support at home and abroad during the 2023 Women's World Cup, jointly hosted by Australia and New Zealand. The team reached the semi-finals, where they lost to England. Source: Getty / The Washington Post

A joint statement by the four UK national associations described the announcement as "a landmark moment".

The US previously sole-hosted the Women's World Cup in 1999 and 2003. England has never hosted a Women's World Cup. In the men's event, England hosted for the only time in 1966.

The US co-hosted this year's men's World Cup, with the majority of matches being played on US soil, including the final at the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, which was won by Spain.

The 2023 Women's World Cup in Australia and New Zealand was the first to be held by more than one nation. Next year's event will be held in Brazil and will feature 32 teams.

Spain are the Women's World Cup holders after defeating England in the 2023 final in Sydney.

The draw for the 2027 Women's World Cup will take place on 11 December in Rio de Janeiro. The US and England are among the nations aiming to secure qualification for the finals before then.

Infantino said Monday's Congress was organised "to celebrate women's football" and was "dedicated exclusively to that".

He therefore did not address his bid for re-election as the head of world football's governing body.

The election will take place at the next FIFA Congress in the Moroccan capital Rabat in March, with France's Philippe Diallo and Japan's Kozo Tashima standing against the incumbent.

title: After fleeing war in Ukraine, Anatolii found himself trapped in Australia's 'crazy' rental crisis
text:
IN BRIEF The Rental Affordability Index says there is no affordable market in Australia, despite slight improvements in 2025.

Regional affordability improved, yet rents nationwide still cost at least 23 per cent of income.

When Russian forces invaded Ukraine, Anatolii Vaishengolts left behind his home and travelled through several countries before he reached Australia.

Four years on, the 22-year-old is safe in Perth, but now finds himself facing a different challenge: Australia's rental crisis.

"The housing is crazy," Vaishengolts told SBS News.

He's inspected rentals advertised as a fully furnished room near the beach with a good view, but discovered little more than a mattress and a table.

Another, he described as looking like a Soviet-era "haunted house".

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"I was running away from it ... like a maniac," he said.

After several disappointments, he considered a more expensive property with a pool and spa that appeared well maintained, only to discover it was available for a single tenant and not suitable for him and his girlfriend.

Simply securing a room to rent has proved a costly challenge — with the city now officially the least affordable capital in the country for renters.

Anatolii Vaishengolts says finding secure and affordable housing in Perth has become a battle of its own. Source: SBS News / Christopher Tan

How is rental affordability across Australia?

Despite a slight improvement in prices since 2025, no areas of Australia are affordable, according to the national Rental Affordability Index released on Tuesday.

Homes across the country now cost at least 23 per cent of the household income.

The outlook is even worse in capital cities — in Sydney, Perth and Hobart, the figures soar past 30 per cent.

Rental prices are considered "acceptable" if they are between 20 and 25 per cent of household income, and "affordable" if they are below that.

Perth, once more affordable than Sydney, overtook it three years ago to become the country's least affordable capital city. It's remained there ever since.

Virginia Lord, a 63 year-old great grandmother, is picking up extra shifts as a ward worker in a Sydney hospital just to afford her sharehouse rent and family days out.

She now pays $400 a week in rent for her space in a two-bedroom home, which she shares with a colleague 20 minutes from their St Leonards workplace.

About $1,000 hits her bank account each week. Her rent is considered severely unaffordable by national standards.

"Unfortunately, sometimes life is very hard, and you have to give things up," Lord told the Australian Associated Press.

Virginia Lord, 63, works two jobs to afford her sharehouse room in Sydney's north. Source: AAP / Damian Shaw

Sydney's affordability has improved by 1 per cent since 2025 as property prices have declined, offering a glimmer of hope for those struggling to pay their bills.

All capitals besides Canberra and Adelaide improved in affordability, as did all regional areas.

Lord said she hoped the government would consider renewed policies to bring prices down further, particularly if the economy entered a recession.

Government urged to 'intervene earlier'

The report also called for better affordability in places where people work, adding to an ongoing federal push.

"When working Australians can no longer afford to live in the communities where they are needed, housing stress increases and pressure on government housing assistance grows," it said.

"If Australia is to reduce long-term demand for social housing and homelessness services, it must intervene earlier in the housing continuum by protecting and increasing the supply of genuinely affordable housing."

But that cannot be achieved purely through government means, the report said.

The Business Council of Co-operative and Mutuals, which oversees housing co-ops across the country, has received the backing this month of major mutual banks to be used in the creation of more homes.

It hopes to eventually build up to 17,500 new homes per year, most of which will be rented out below market rate, where people can live long-term in secure housing.

Australia does not have a nationally consistent way to identify and track affordable rentals, which Housing All Australians, one of the report's authors, is calling to have fixed.

title: Pacific nations forge new climate alliances after COP31 collapse
text:
IN BRIEF Australia is facing criticism after COP31 negotiations collapsed over disagreements on fossil fuels.

Tuvalu says it will plan a new summit focused on a just transition away from fossil fuels.

Pacific island nations have been left to form their own climate coalitions after the COP31 conference in Türkiye failed to deliver a global agreement.

A failure to mention fossil fuels' climate impact torpedoed the summit's draft agreement, giving Australia — and Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen, who led the negotiations — a black eye after it lobbied hard to host the talks and voice Pacific concerns.

"Tuvalu cannot accept this as the final scenario, as a matter of survival," Tuvalu's climate change and environment minister Maina Talia said in a statement after negotiations collapsed.

"We will not allow inaction and obstruction to dampen our resolve. We will advance where we can with those willing to show up."

Australia leading the conference's negotiations will likely sit uncomfortably with Pacific allies, University of Canberra environment expert Sotiris Vardoulakis said.

"We should be taking some of the blame as a fossil fuel exporting country, one of the major exporters of coal and gas," he told the Australian Associated Press (AAP).

Vardoulakis added Australian domestic policy's contradiction with its climate ambitions had long plagued the nation's standing in the region.

"The lack of consistency between climate diplomacy and export policies in Australia ... that will be concerning for Pacific countries," he said.

Despite poor attendance at the preliminary event, the Pacific region remained central to conversations in Türkiye, according to ANU researcher Llewelyn Hughes.

COP31's pact was watered down to appease resource-reliant nations and then panned by the European Union and other parties — disagreements Bowen said were insurmountable.

Fijian climate minister Lynda Tabuya was deeply disappointed an agreement wasn't reached but acknowledged Bowen's burden.

"You have tried your utmost best, and we have seen it," Tabuya told the summit on Sunday.

"The failure here is not yours to carry. It is the responsibility of all parties."

The Marshall Islands delegation was less charitable.

title: How not getting enough sleep could affect your memory
text:
Have you recently walked into a room and forgotten why you went there? Or find yourself reading the same email three times because nothing seems to stick? Perhaps you’ve struggled to remember the name of a friend of a friend.

Sound familiar? We’ve all been there. Most of us attribute these moments to being tired, stressed or having too much on our minds. That’s usually the case.

But the fog may indicate that our brain is missing its overnight maintenance.

Sleep isn’t just a time when the brain shuts down. During sleep, the brain reviews the day’s experiences, strengthens important memories and clears out waste.

If sleep is disrupted, these processes don’t work as well. This can affect how we learn and remember things both now and in the future.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The brain’s overnight cleaning service

Scientists have long known that poor sleep is associated with an increased risk of memory problems and Alzheimer’s disease later in life.

Research also shows people who get poor-quality sleep have higher levels of the two proteins linked to Alzheimer’s disease, amyloid-beta and tau.

Emerging evidence offers further insights into the link between sleep and memory by comparing what happens after a normal night’s sleep with a night of complete sleep deprivation.

After a normal night’s sleep, participants had much higher levels of amyloid beta and tau in their blood than after staying up all night. That might sound bad at first, but researchers believe the brain was clearing these proteins and moving them into the blood for removal.

This process likely occurs through the glymphatic system, often described as the brain’s cleaning or drainage network. Much like a city’s overnight cleaning crew, the glymphatic system helps wash away waste that builds up during the day. Sleep appears to be the time when this cleaning system works most efficiently.

So, a night of healthy sleep may help the brain clear away some of the substances linked to memory decline.

How the day shapes the night

Sleep and memory are a two-way street. Sleep influences our memories, and our memories influence our sleep.

A recent study explored this connection in mice. Researchers exposed one group of mice to positive experiences and another group to stressful experiences.

During sleep, the mice appeared to replay memories of their day. Mice that experienced stressful events showed more fragmented and disrupted sleep. Mice that had positive experiences slept more soundly and consistently.

READ MORE How seasons and even days of the week impact sleep

These memories seemed to directly affect sleep quality. But when the researchers reduced the activity of the brain cells storing stressful memories, sleep became stable again.

This study was in animals and can’t be generalised to humans. But it may give us some clues about how stress and poor sleep get trapped in a vicious cycle: a tough day can lead to restless sleep. Poor sleep then makes us feel more sensitive, stressed and less able to cope the next day.

Sleep disorders affecting memory

Obstructive sleep apnoea is a disorder that affects 9–38 per cent of the population, causing breathing pauses during sleep.

These breathing pauses often cause brief awakenings and significantly interrupt a person’s sleep pattern, but they often go unnoticed overnight.

Although brief, they disrupt normal sleep and keep the brain from getting the deep, restful sleep it needs.

Research shows people with more severe sleep apnoea perform worse on tests of memory and thinking. These memory differences remained even after accounting for factors such as depression and other health conditions.

So if you’re having problems with your memory, talk to your doctor about your sleep, as well as other symptoms.

Small changes can make a big difference

The good news is that sleep is one of the few risk factors for memory problems we can actually address.

There is no magic fix, but a few simple habits can help you sleep better:

Keep your bedroom dark, quiet and comfortable

Try to go to bed and wake up at consistent times each day

Avoid caffeine in the afternoon and evening, at least six hours prior to bedtime

Limit alcohol three to four hours before bedtime, as it can disrupt sleep quality

Create a relaxing wind-down routine, such as reading, meditation, stretching or a warm bath

Seek medical advice if you regularly snore loudly, wake up gasping, feel excessively sleepy during the day or suspect you may have sleep apnoea or another sleep disorder

Each night, your brain does much more than rest. It strengthens memories, organises what you’ve learned, processes emotions and clears away waste that can build up over time.

title: How the COP31 agreement fell apart — and what happens next
text:
Two days after the COP31 global climate summit was supposed to finish, the talks in Antalya, Türkiye, have come to an end — but not as we might have hoped.

Agreement simply could not be reached. The sticking point was the omission of fossil fuels in draft texts. The European Union led a revolt, shattering the consensus needed to adopt the cover text proposed by the Turkish and Australian conveners.

In a year of unprecedented climate disasters, a supercharged El Niño and as the world heads inevitably past 1.5C of warming, the EU and other nations said that the international process did not meet the moment.

Some coverage has suggested the rejection of the cover text is a sign the entire summit was a failure. This isn’t quite right.

These texts have always been add-ons to the formal negotiation process. Countries have regularly agreed these political, overarching statements, particularly since the Glasgow meeting in 2021, but they are not a requirement.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Its failure does not signal the end of the COP process — or the breakdown of the Paris Agreement. What it may mean is that international climate cooperation will look different from this point onwards.

No mention of the 'F' word

For many observers, the litmus test for success at COP31 was whether countries could make any headway on the root cause of climate change — fossil fuels. Unfortunately, fossil fuels proved unmentionable.

Three years ago at COP28 in Dubai, countries agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels", marking the first time fossil fuels had explicitly been mentioned in an official decision text in decades of negotiations.

The Dubai text was hailed as “the beginning of the end of the fossil fuel era". But there was little sign that hope would be realised in Türkiye.

In a repeat of last year’s fraught negotiations at COP30 in Brazil, major fossil fuel producing nations Saudi Arabia and Russia banded together to block any reference in the negotiating outcomes and proposed cover text.

Australia and Türkiye proposed a compromise — no fossil fuel language in exchange for support for electrification “with the greatest possible use of clean energy".

This seemed to get Saudi Arabia over the line but drew backlash from the European Union, Panama, the Marshall Islands, Vanuatu, and Belize, who rejected the cover text.

Brazil took a different approach to the same problem last year. In a bid to break the deadlock, Brazil committed to develop a global strategy to phase out fossil fuels outside the formal negotiating agenda.

The roadmap was launched at this year’s summit in Türkiye and managed to attract support from big fossil fuel producers such as India, Germany and Nigeria. Countries across the European Union are launching similar roadmaps.

Frustration over fossil fuels at COP31 is likely to lead more nations to go outside official talks to progress phase-out efforts. Earlier this year, 57 nations attended the first conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels in Santa Marta, Colombia. Another meeting is planned for next year, co-hosted by Tuvalu and Ireland.

Neither the Turkish hosts nor their Australian partners seemed keen to mention fossil fuels. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan was untroubled by the optics of announcing two huge new oilfields in Türkiye in his speech at the summit opening. While Prime Minister Anthony Albanese highlighted the existential risks to Pacific countries from climate change, he made no commitment to stop approving new Australian coal and gas projects.

Both leaders much preferred to talk about electrification, namely the flagship "35 by 35" electrification pledge. The goal here is to boost electricity’s share of final energy use globally from around 23 per cent at present to 35 per cent by 2035.

Efforts to embed this goal in the cover text failed. But the electrification pledge drew strong support outside official negotiations. More than 75 countries and 180 businesses signed on, including the European Union and China.

The 'COP of action' fails to deliver

This year’s climate summit was billed as an "implementation COP", focused on delivering the pledges countries had already made to address climate change.

Overseen by Australia in its role as "president of negotiations", the formal talks largely focused on the actions countries are taking to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change, whether their response is sufficiently urgent and whether funds aimed at supporting the most vulnerable countries are adequate.

It was abundantly obvious that longstanding divisions had not been overcome. Developed countries called for emissions to be cut faster, while developing countries responded by pointing to a lack of financial support to do so.

African countries, in particular, stressed that an “implementation COP” was meaningless if rich nations failed to provide the actual resources needed to act.

Despite the general gloom, these talks did achieve progress in a few areas. Nations moved forwards on supporting a just transition (shifting to clean energy fairly) via a “phased approach”, as well as improving alignment in climate adaptation, which will help the poorest nations to implement their adaptation plans.

But broader efforts to find a way forward on the Paris Agreement’s Global Goal on Adaptation were left unresolved.

Decisions stalled in many negotiating rooms in the face of hard “red lines” declared by different blocs of countries.

Countries failed to reach any agreement on the vital question of cutting emissions, after Saudi Arabia and Russia blocked a proposed decision. Both are among the world’s top fossil fuel exporting nations.

This failure has left the world without any dedicated negotiating process on cutting emissions under the Paris Agreement. It's possible nations could agree to renew a work program on climate mitigation at next year’s COP32 talks in Ethiopia.

What about money for adaptation?

Who pays for the costs of climate change has long been a contentious point. Developing countries face the brunt of damage from climate change, but have emitted far less — and have much less money to spend on adaptation.

Ahead of COP31, EU climate commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said talks on new climate finance commitments were "dead in the water". He urged delegates to focus on implementing existing pledges rather than try for fresh funding.

The summit failed to meet even these low expectations. No concrete progress was achieved on the goal of tripling funds for climate adaptation pledged last year at COP30 in Brazil.

Ahead of the summit, the Australian government flagged the need to boost global contributions to the official Pacific climate fund.

This, too, didn’t eventuate. Rich nations — including Australia — merely re-announced their existing pledges, leaving the Pacific fund $450 million short of its 2026 target of $749 million.

Ironically, the most notable pledge came from Solomon Islands, a small Pacific nation. Prime Minister Matthew Wale pledged $600,000 to the global Green Climate Fund. "The Pacific did not create this crisis," he declared. "But we will not stand by and wait for others to act."

A few new commitments arrived by the end of the two week summit from nations such as Canada and Norway.

Defending the science

Unusually, climate science was front and centre at COP31.

This year, a small bloc of fossil fuel-producing countries has been obstructing the publication of key scientific reports from the world’s leading body of climate scientists, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.

READ MORE The Australians pushing back against a 40 million tonne emissions threat

This year marks the first UN summit since it was officially confirmed the world will overshoot the Paris Agreement’s 1.5C goal by 2030.

With the collapse of support for the cover text, statements supporting release of the latest climate science didn’t get approval. All that remained were technical conclusions which "expressed utmost concern" that climate impacts will continue to increase with every increment of global warming.

Australia on the global stage

COP31 gave Australia a unique global role. After being outmanoeuvred in their bid to host the summit, Australia secured a role in overseeing negotiations.

Climate and Energy Minister Chris Bowen and his team had the unenviable task of seeking consensus between 195 countries and the European Union.

After the cover text was rejected, Bowen declared Australia had left "nothing on the field" but had faced "unbridgeable red lines".

Hours beforehand, Fijian climate minister Lynda Tabuya acknowledged Bowen’s efforts, noting the failure was "not yours to carry […] it is the responsibility of all parties".

Are COP summits still worthwhile?

This year’s climate summit took the unenviable record of the longest ever. With consensus seemingly impossible, some civil society representatives dubbed it “the worst COP ever.”

Outgoing UN secretary-general António Guterres blamed “powerful fossil fuel interests”, including fossil fuel exporters and corporate lobbyists.

Some nations are now calling for urgent reform to negotiations long paralysed by vetoes and disconnected from science.

Unfortunately, any change to official voting processes would itself require a consensus decision.

Consensus is hard to achieve, but powerful. The power of the Paris Agreement draws on the fact it represents the view of nearly every country — big or small, rich or poor.

COP31 President Murat Kurum began the summit expressing hopes this year’s talks would leave a legacy of “working together.”

That was a false hope. A more realistic hope is that the collapse of consensus may be the shock the world needs to change course.

As former UN climate chief Christiana Figueres has said, we should not see the refusal of more than 130 countries to sign an inadequate deal as a failure. Rather, it might be “a sign of courage”.

title: Small businesses spared from online crackdown as crunch time looms for government
text:
In brief Low-risk businesses will be exempt from the government's Digital Duty of Care requirements.

The government still has to reach a deal with the Greens to get the bill through the Senate.

Small businesses will be carved out of the government's plans for online safety crackdowns, as ministers push to get legislation across the line during the final sitting week of the year.

Low-risk business websites will be exempt from Digital Duty of Care requirements if the bill passes, Communications Minister Anika Wells confirmed in a statement.

"The intention of the Digital Duty of Care is to put the onus on tech companies to protect Australians from online harms before they occur — not to create additional burden for low-risk small businesses," she said on Monday.

The onus would be placed back on technology companies to prevent foreseeable harms online.

Labor hopes to reach an agreement with the Greens, who hold the balance of power in the Senate, after the Coalition confirmed it would not support the bill.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has returned from a series of overseas summits to crunch time in parliament, but faces an uphill battle as his popularity has taken a nosedive.

Separately, Labor will rely on the Opposition to endorse plans for gas companies to set aside up to 20 per cent of their exports for Australian use after a foiled attempt to ram the legislation through the Senate.

The Coalition is not satisfied the bill will ensure future investment or new export opportunities for gas producers after Labor caved on demands to effectively exclude Western Australia from the national scheme.

But there's no hope the Coalition will back a minimum 30 per cent tax on some discretionary trusts — a levy the Greens have said must not exempt funds for tax-exempt organisations such as private schools or religious institutions.

The minor party could also decide whether a 50 per cent capital gains tax discount is reinstated for innovative start-ups.

A last-minute counter-proposal from independent MP Allegra Spender has threatened to send that legislation to a summer inquiry.

title: 'True icon': Music journalist Molly Meldrum dies aged 83
text:
IN BRIEF Meldrum died early on Monday morning at Richmond's Epworth Hospital.

The legendary music journalist was the beloved face of ABC's Countdown in the 1970s and 80s.

Legendary journalist Ian "Molly" Meldrum has died at the age of 83 after making and breaking music careers for decades.

He died early on Monday morning at Epworth Hospital in Richmond, Melbourne, after a long illness, his family said in a statement.

"He was deeply loved by his long-term partner, Yan Wongngam, his family and all who knew him," they said.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has also paid tribute to Meldrum.

"With an interview style that was inimitable and an enthusiasm that was uncontainable, Molly Meldrum loved music almost as much as we loved him," Albanese said in a social media post.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"On Countdown and beyond, he championed Australian artists and brought international acts to our shores. He gave new artists a leg up and established artists a welcoming embrace.

"And over the years, as he implored us to do ourselves a favour, he became a central part of the Australian soundtrack. We were lucky to have him."

His longtime friend and manager, Mark Klemens of Profile Talent Management, said Australia had lost a "true icon".

"A man who opened doors for so many and entertained millions of people here and around the world," Klemens said on Monday.

Meldrum faced a serious health battle after falling from a ladder in 2011 and has had several health issues since. Source: AAP / James Ross

"He was unconventional and wonderfully unpredictable, but always caring, always funny and always down to earth, with a passion the rest of us could only envy.

"He made the most of his life, and boy, was it a full one. Rest in peace, Molly."

Who was Molly Meldrum?

Born in the regional Victorian town of Orbost in 1943, Meldrum forged a career in the music industry, becoming the face of ABC's wildly popular Countdown program in the 1970s and 80s.

He was introduced to the music business while working as a roadie for his friend's band, The Groop, and through a weekly column he wrote for the pop music newspaper Go-Set.

His unique, "camp" writing style earned him the nickname Molly from a DJ friend.

He moved to London in the late 1960s, where he met his idols John Lennon and Paul McCartney.

After returning to Australia, Meldrum's major break came in 1974 when he was commissioned to create a music show for the ABC.

Countdown was a phenomenal success and catapulted Meldrum into the spotlight.

Meldrum was a devoted supporter of the St Kilda Football Club. Source: AAP / Rob Prezioso

He became synonymous with the Australian music industry and Countdown acted as a springboard for local bands Skyhooks and Sherbet and international artists including ABBA and Cyndi Lauper.

His laid-back interview style made him the go-to guy for many artists like Elton John and Rod Stewart.

From Bruce Springsteen and Beyonce to Madonna and Michael Jackson, few have had a bad word to say about Meldrum.

"Molly is often the only person in the world who gets the interview," according to Australian music promoter Michael Chugg, who was a close friend of Meldrum's for more than 40 years.

"That's the regard he is held in."

But there was one interview that Meldrum himself admitted didn't go well.

In 1977 he nervously interviewed Prince Charles and was famously reprimanded by the visiting royal for referring to the Queen as "your mum".

While co-hosting Countdown with Dolly Parton, he was starstruck.

"I've never been more nervous doing a show in my life," he told the country music superstar in 1979.

Countdown was cancelled in 1987, but Meldrum had become bigger than the show itself.

Besides fronting Countdown, Meldrum was also known for his success as a music producer.

He worked with Australian star Russell Morris to produce his classic song The Real Thing, while also producing hits for Ronnie Burns, Colleen Hewett, Supernaut and The Ferrets.

In 1985 he hosted the Australian leg of Live Aid, Oz for Africa.

A year later he was made a Member of the Order of Australia for services to the fostering of international relief and to youth.

He added an ARIA Special Achievement Award for services to the industry to the collection in 1993.

Other TV appearances included a regular segment on long-running variety show Hey Hey It's Saturday called Molly's Melodrama.

In 2004, he joined Christine Anu and John Paul Young as a judge on Popstars Live, and was also a producer on the series.

Ian 'Molly' Meldrum at his 80th birthday celebration alongside his beloved dog. Source: Getty / Sam Tabone/WireImage

Meldrum faced a serious health battle in December 2011 after falling from a ladder while hanging Christmas decorations. He was placed in an induced coma due to severe head lacerations.

In 2014, he was inducted into the ARIA Hall of Fame and released his autobiography, which he wrote with music journalist Jeff Jenkins.

He was a long-time supporter of the St Kilda AFL team and Melbourne Storm NRL side.

He also loved his string of loyal dogs, who were all named Ziggy.

Meldrum is survived by his brothers, Brian and Robert, and by Morgan, whom he helped raise and regarded as his son, along with Morgan's wife, Crystal, and their son, Jason, who Meldrum cherished as a grandson.

His long-time partner Yan Wongngam cared for Meldrum with great love and devotion, especially through his final years.

Meldrum's family have requested privacy as they grieve.

title: Liberals, Greens label Labor 'worse than disappointing' over role in COP31 breakdown
text:
In brief A final agreement was dramatically rejected at COP31 on Sunday after the conference ran two days over schedule.

Türkiye and Australia had tried to rally support behind a global goal to electrify the world economy.

The Opposition leader has called on Labor's Chris Bowen to resign after the COP31 climate talks ended without agreement, while the Greens have criticised what they called "a comprehensive failure of leadership from Labor".

Bowen, the climate change and energy minister who served as COP31 negotiations chair under a co-hosting deal struck with Türkiye, unsuccessfully sought to broker consensus among nearly 200 nations.

However, he ultimately conceded he could not overcome what he called "unbridgeable red lines", partly related to the inclusion or omission of references to fossil fuels in the agreement, which was dramatically rejected on Sunday.

It was a chaotic finale to a United Nations climate summit that ran two days over schedule, underscoring the strains on diplomacy in an increasingly fractured world.

Bowen's Liberal energy counterpart, Dan Tehan, said if Bowen doesn't resign, the prime minister should sack him.
