Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Chris Bowen should resign today," Tehan said in a statement.

"Australian taxpayers have funded Chris Bowen’s $150m COP pretensions, only for the so-called president to embarrass Australia on the world stage by making jokes about his penis. Of course, the one thing Chris Bowen has not failed to do is spend taxpayers’ money."

Tehan was referring to a gaffe by Bowen and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, who were recorded joking about phone radiation and penises while waiting for a meeting to begin at the conference. Albanese later apologised for the hot-mic incident.

From the start, the Coalition has been critical of Australia's bid to host the summit and has lashed the costs of co-hosting the talks.

Liberal leader Angus Taylor later echoed the call for Bowen to resign, saying "he's not up to the job".

"We should scrap net zero, that what should happen tomorrow and we should unleash the natural resources we have in this country, our oil, our coal, our gas, our uranium."

Meanwhile, Greens leader David Shoebridge said the government was "doing what it can to destroy the global action we need for a safe climate."

"At the end of COP 31, we have the Albanese Labor government choosing to side with Saudi Arabia and Trump, and not mention fossil fuels, rather than back in Europe and our Pacific neighbours.

"This is worse than disappointing."

Australian climate groups have also expressed disappointment at the lack of agreement, with some putting the blame on Bowen and Albanese.

"As president of negotiations, Australia failed to broker an agreement when wealthy nations blocked progress on climate finance," Denise Cauchi, CEO of Climate Action Network Australia, said.

"Instead of implementing the transition away from fossil fuels agreed to three years ago and the just transition agreed last year, Australia and Türkiye caved to 700 carbon capture lobbyists and almost gifted industry the biggest loophole for coal, oil and gas expansion in the history of COP."

Former Greens leader and CEO of Australian Conservation Foundation Adam Bandt was also scathing.

"Countries understandably rejected an Australia-led deal that failed to even mention the main causes of the climate crisis, let alone address them," Bandt said.

"The prime minister's snub of the UN secretary-general by failing to mention coal and gas in his speech set the tone early in this summit. The UN secretary-general urged Australia and Türkiye to make this the COP that staves off climate collapse by reining in coal and gas, but the prime minister refused to listen."

UN secretary-general António Guterres, who urged nations to send fossil fuels "the way of the dinosaurs" during a fiery appearance at COP31, expressed deep dismay as the talks broke down.

"I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands," the outgoing UN chief said in a statement.

"Unfortunately, we were unable to reach agreement on a cover decision ... And that's disappointing. Very disappointing," Bowen, told reporters.

More than 49 hours after the summit was supposed to end, COP31 president and Turkish environment minister Murat Kurum banged the gavel to conclude the marathon talks.

'Fraught geopolitical environment'

Bowen said the summit backdrop was "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory" as soaring energy prices and fallout from the Middle East war complicated the search for unity.

Under pressure to show progress in a year of climate-linked disasters from Europe to Nepal, Bowen sought an overarching "cover decision" to prove countries were still united in tackling the crisis.

But his plan unravelled as familiar fault lines emerged over fossil fuels, with the EU and Saudi Arabia locking horns over the pace of the shift away from coal, oil and gas.

The negotiations stalled as oil-producing states blocked any mention of phasing out fossil fuels in the final deal.

"We will not endorse a cover decision ... that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change," said Ireland's climate minister, Darragh O'Brien, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency.

"And we will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel."

Panama, Vanuatu and the Marshall Islands also objected and, as the deal imploded, COP31 became the longest climate summit on record.

'World cannot afford a repeat'

The outcome revived memories of the failed Copenhagen summit of 2009 and raised fresh doubts about the effectiveness of climate diplomacy.

"It certainly fell short today," said UN climate chief Simon Stiell, describing progress over the marathon fortnight of negotiations in Antalya as "limited".

"The world cannot afford a repeat."

Frustrated by the inertia, countries are pushing ahead outside the COP process.

Around 60 countries joined a first-of-its-kind conference in April on phasing out fossil fuels while several nations at COP31 unveiled their own plans to exit coal, oil and gas.

In a last-ditch bid for compromise, COP31 hosts Türkiye and Australia could only muster a veiled reference to fossil fuels in the final text.

But the pact also took fire for retaining a call to expand carbon capture — a costly technology championed by the fossil fuel industry.

title: More Australians are avoiding the doctor. What's the real cost?
text:
IN BRIEF Half of Australians are opting to forgo health care to save money, according to new research.

Almost 20 per cent of those surveyed by researchers were not satisfied with previous healthcare services.

Half of Australians are putting up with pain rather than see a doctor or dentist because of the cost.

A survey of more than 5,000 people found almost half decided to forgo certain healthcare interventions over the last 12 months.

Lack of affordability was the most common reason why people delayed or went without care, according to the Consumers Health Forum of Australia's national consumer sentiment survey, released on Monday.

More than two-thirds of that group put off seeing a dentist, close to half did not fill a prescription and a third did not see a doctor, the 80-page report found.

Consumers Health Forum of Australia chief executive Elizabeth Deveny said the findings described a health system splitting in two.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"We have a health system where there are the haves and the have-nots. The gap between them is where people are getting hurt," she said.

"Healthcare decisions are made at the kitchen table and weighed against rent, groceries and everything else due that week. For a lot of people, choices are becoming impossible."

Dental care in particular was identified as the most expensive health service, with nine in 10 respondents agreeing that it should be considered part of Medicare and partially subsidised.

Close to six in 10 had delayed or avoided dental care and reported pain, difficulty eating and even losing teeth.

Brisbane resident Gaylene Smith, 74, has been supporting her sister in Darwin who was first diagnosed with breast cancer in 2018.

She praised the medical team surrounding her but worried that patients were "fading away" under the strain of rising costs and being unable to keep up with medical bills.

Her sister needed medication to treat psoriasis, which developed as a side effect of the cancer therapy and cost about $4,000 per month before recently being listed on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme.

"It would have been nice for there to have been a process [so] that she could have accessed that either cheaply or cheaper than $4,000 a month," Smith told the Australian Associated Press news agency.

The survey findings also suggested that healthcare experiences were shaped not only by financial resources and health needs, but also by whether services were accessible and culturally appropriate.

Despite the access and equity challenges, 81 per cent of respondents who had received health care said they were satisfied with their care.

title: The data centre lobby's growing influence: 100 meetings, millions in political payments
text:
IN BRIEF A new report has found 11 data centre companies and their lobbying firms spent $3.4 million in the past four years.

It says the payments went predominantly to the Labor Party and the Australian Business Council.

Data centre companies have held more than 100 meetings with state premiers and ministers in the past three years, and given $3.4 million to parties and industry bodies.

That's according to Transparency International, which has partially captured the industry's lobbying efforts and people-to-people links as the sector's footprint expands across Australia to at least 283 planned or operational data centres.

The information is only partially captured because Western Australia, South Australia, the Northern Territory and the federal government do not give access to ministerial diaries, meaning the engagement might be the tip of the iceberg.

Queensland's David Crisafulli has held 13 meetings with data centre executives since 2023, the most of any premier captured by the figures.

They included three meetings with ADC in May 2026 and three meetings with NextDC in three weeks from August 2026, just before Queensland announced a fast-track data centre approval process.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Transparency International Australia chief executive Clancy Moore said the level of access to decision-makers might concern Australians, given polling shows deep divides on the merits of such centres.

"They have huge amounts of resources, access to ministers, access to third-party lobbyists and that gives them a huge advantage, particularly when local community groups are being shut out from decision-making processes," he told the Australian Associated Press (AAP) news agency.

"This erodes trust in our democracy and risks decisions favouring private not public interests."

The report tallies payments of $3.4 million from 11 data centre companies and their lobbying firms in the past four years, predominantly to the Labor Party and Australian Business Council.

Several data centre firms gave six-figure amounts, including Microsoft ($414,700), Macquarie Technology ($346,900), Goodman ($308,000) and Amazon ($254,346), while Anacta, a lobbying firm for Anthropic, gave $468,107.

A large chunk of the funding was not categorised as a donation but declared in other ways, suggesting membership of a party's business forum or seats at events involving senior party members.

Moore said these donations created a perception of "pay to play".

The watchdog organisation believes lawmakers risk "policy capture" by the industry and wants improved disclosure of lobbying, staff movements between government and industry and funding.

Independent Kooyong MP Monique Ryan will launch a reform push for just that on Monday, although her legislation will fail without government support.

Ryan's national lobbying bill would replace the existing code of conduct with a legislated scheme, including beefed-up reporting requirements that also capture in-house lobbyists.

"We need to know who ministers meet with, where, when and why because that will go a long way toward restoring trust in evidence-based decision-making," she told AAP.

Federal ministers currently dodge requests to provide their diaries under freedom of information processes.

The bill also enforces a stand-down period for ministers, political staffers and high-ranking public servants taking lobbying jobs after public office.

Transparency International details examples of the "revolving door" between government and industry, including a new hire for OpenAI plucked from the office of AI in the prime minister's department.

"People lose faith in government decision-making when they see people go straight from the positions where those decisions are made into the industries that commercially benefit," Ryan said.

She hoped to meet with Attorney-General Michelle Rowland in the coming week to garner support.

title: Australia's first GLP-1 weight-loss tablets are here. How do they compare to injections?
text:
IN BRIEF Australia's first GLP-1s in tablet form have hit the market.

The two types available have differing pros and cons.

The arrival of GLP-1 tablets is giving Australians more choice in weight-loss treatment, with experts saying the new medications have broadly similar effects to existing injections.

The Wegovy tablet, made by Danish pharmaceutical company Novo Nordisk, became the first of its kind to be cleared by Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) this month and landed on pharmacy shelves on Friday.

Until now, GLP-1 medications approved for weight management in Australia have been administered through weekly injections.

A second weight-loss pill, Foundayo, made by US pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly, has also received TGA approval.

Both medications work by mimicking the action of GLP-1, a hormone released by the gut after eating that helps regulate blood sugar levels and appetite.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Use of Wegovy, Ozempic and other GLP-1 drugs for diabetes has surged in recent years. In Australia, sales of these medications increased almost tenfold between May 2020 and April 2025, according to research from the University of New South Wales, with at least half a million people estimated to be regularly using them.

While these drugs were traditionally used for diabetes, some have since been approved for weight management.

Teacher and mother-of-six Kim Roberts has been giving herself weekly weight-loss drug injections for the past three years after a heart attack led to the discovery of a genetic cholesterol condition.

She plans to switch to taking Wegovy as a daily tablet.

"It will just fit in with what I do on a day-to-day basis," she told the Australian Associated Press.

The 46-year-old said the drug has helped her to lose around 30kg, learn to eat better and manage her condition.

Mother-of-six and teacher Kim Roberts is looking forward to the weight loss drug in pill format. Source: AAP / Supplied/PR Image

How does it compare to injections?

Professor Priya Sumithran, head of the obesity and metabolic medicine group at Monash University, said the new tablets could appeal to people who have been reluctant to use injectable medications.

While the pills offer a new way to take the drug, she said there are few significant differences in the way they work and the associated side effects.

"I think the considerations would mostly be up to personal preference — whether you prefer to take a once-a-week injection, [or] whether you prefer to take a once-a-day tablet," she said.

Drugs such as Wegovy and Ozempic have been available in Australia as injectables only. Source: AAP / Jason Bergman/Sipa USA

The tablets also have similar side effects to injectable GLP-1 medications, with nausea, vomiting and indigestion among the most common.

Louise Baur, an expert in child and adolescent obesity at the University of Sydney, said a daily medication can bring its own challenges and lifestyle adjustments for some.

"You have to take [the Wegovy pill] at least half an hour before eating, and so that means a routine that you have to get into," she said.

Unlike Wegovy, Foundayo can be taken at any time of day without the same restrictions.

Experts have cautioned against viewing GLP-1 medications as a quick fix for weight loss, but rather as part of a broader approach to managing obesity that includes health eating, physical activity and ongoing medical support.

How much do they cost?

The price of Wegovy tablets varies by dose, costing between $260 and $395 a month.

It's not listed on Australia's Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme, though it was recommended by an advisory committee nearly a year ago.

The federal government is in negotiations with Wegovy's manufacturer to bring it onto the scheme for a small cohort of patients.

It would bring the price down to $25 per script or $7.70 for concession card holders.

Source: SBS News

Terri-Lynne South, a GP with a special interest in obesity management at the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners, said affordability remains a barrier for patients.

"Like the injectable, it's only available on private prescription. Until obesity medicines are subsidised, access will be determined by what people can afford rather than by clinical need," she said.

"Obesity is a chronic disease, and weight regain is common when treatment stops, so it is important to discuss the long-term plan with patients, including cost, before starting."

What's next for weight-loss medications?

Sumithran said nearly 30 medications are undergoing late-stage clinical trials, with some combining GLP-1 with other hormones to potentially improve their effectiveness or target particular health conditions.

She said the expanding range of treatments could eventually allow doctors to better tailor medications to individual patients.

"I think the interesting thing about those additional hormones is what specific benefits we will get from those," she said.

Researchers are also investigating the use of existing medications in children and adolescents.

Baur said two recent studies had examined the use of GLP-1 medications in children and adolescents, including the first trial of injectable semaglutide in children aged six to 12.

However, she said, the development of new medications needs to be accompanied by greater efforts to improve access to affordable treatment and support and tackle the underlying drivers of obesity.

She called for a future in which people living with obesity could access effective treatment without experiencing stigma, including within the healthcare system.

— With additional reporting by the Australian Associated Press.

title: COP31 might have failed yet fossil fuels are done for
text:

Letters NationalVictoriaLetters COP31 might have failed yet fossil fuels are done for November 24, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Matt Golding To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. CLIMATE CHANGE Saudi Arabia and Russia and other fossil fuel exporters won’t sign on to transitioning away from them. Who cares? The direction is set.

Demand for coal, oil and gas will crumble for lack of buyers who will be choosing the cheapest source of energy the world has ever seen.

Countries are increasing their use of rooftop solar panels and batteries, electric vehicles for transport, and large-scale solar and wind power. As old power stations die, replacement will come from the cheapest way to provide that energy.

Renewable energy is so far ahead as the most cost-effective and efficient, that all other bets will be off.

Fossil fuel reduction will happen in parallel with electrification. The job will be done.

Carolyn Ingvarson, Canterbury Betrayal of nations with lightest climate impact

Re “There’s no getting around the scope of this failure‴⁣⁣ (24/11). Nick O’Malley’s article demonstrates the disconnect between the need to accelerate containing the consequences of the changing climate and the dependence and development of fossil fuels.

The transition away from fossil fuels is necessary given the impact of global warming. It is well documented by science that the world is heading to 1.5c of warming within a few years.

The failure of a resolution at COP31 is also a betrayal to those with the lightest footprint such as the Pacific islands who have no financial commitment to help them mitigate its impact.

There is also a contradiction in Australia’s advocacy for electrification while continuing to invest in new fossil fuel extraction. Perhaps the failure of COP31 will energise demand that the world change direction, and it will be led by those most affected.

Judith Morrison, Nunawading

Advertisement

Coalition’s mixed signals on net zero target

After the failure of COP31 in Turkiye to reach consensus for an overarching agreement, the Coalition has blamed Chris Bowen, the president of negotiations, for that disappointing outcome.

Given the primary reason was the unwillingness of the world’s largest oil producers to have a reduction of fossil fuel included in any agreement, coupled with the fact that the Coalition’s climate and energy policy includes the abandonment of net zero emissions targets and prioritises fossil fuel over renewables, I would have expected the Coalition to praise Bowen rather than call for his resignation.

Kevin Bailey, Croydon COP31 has issued a massive reality check

In contrast to the uniformly pessimistic tone of Nick O’Malley’s assessment (“There’s no getting around the scope of this failure”, 24/11), a Letters correspondent (24/11) argues that the “failure to produce a ‘consensus’ agreement at COP31 is the best possible outcome”. I’m inclined to agree.

More than 130 countries refused to be complicit in a compromised statement that pretended fossil fuels didn’t exist, much less create havoc with the climate and nature’s ecosystems.

Their defiant stance exposes fossil fuel nations like Saudi Arabia and Russia, and indeed COP co-hosts Australia and Turkiye, for what they are, ruthless bandits holding the world to ransom.

In short, COP31 has issued a massive reality check. The majority of the world’s nations will double down on efforts to diminish their dependence on fossil fuels and accelerate the process of electrification.

It’s only fair for the prime minister to defend Chris Bowen’s leadership at the global conference (“PM defends Bowen after collapse of climate talks” 24/11), but his comradely words would have more credibility if they were matched by a decisive end to his government’s indefensible approval of more and more coal and gas projects around the country.

Tom Knowles, Parkville THE FORUM Asylum prejudice

Re “Bring back asylums: Why experts and the lord mayor want psychiatric hospitals to return”, 24/11) the final point made is that “both Labor and the Coalition said revisiting asylums was not a priority”.

By using the word asylum, both parties revive the prejudices held against the old-style mental hospitals with their locked wards and institutionalised populations. They tap into some often very negative ideas about what happened in these places.

I have worked in at the old Beechworth Mental Hospital and Training Centre and the very new Bendigo Psychiatric Hospital in the 1970s. The first can still be visited because of its historical architecture, but there is no sign of the second.

I’m sure they weren’t perfect, but when I read about events like those involving mentally unwell people being caught up in violence, either as victims or perpetrators, and the high number of homeless people with mental illness, I rue the day all the mental hospitals were closed. They did provide care and treatment and at the very least, shelter and the basic necessities of life.

I support Monash University mental health researcher David Copolov’s call for the development of modern psychiatric hospitals. What he proposes is a much more modern model of care than that at asylums established in the 19th century. Our mental health services need this extra level of service urgently.

Ruth Hudnott, Canterbury System needs help

The debate about Victoria’s mental health system seems overwhelmingly concerned with what to do with people once they become unwell (″⁣Three decades after Victoria closed its asylums″⁣, 24/11). Far less attention is paid to the kind of society that is making people unwell in the first place.

The British cultural theorist Mark Fisher called this the “privatisation of stress”: the remarkable ideological achievement of turning collective social problems into individual psychological disorders.

We normalise economic insecurity, unaffordable housing, relentless competition and social isolation, then prescribe medication and therapy to those who struggle to cope.

Of course, we need adequately funded mental health services. But perhaps it is time we put our economic and social system on the psychiatrist’s couch, rather than just its casualties.

Fernanda Trecenti, Fitzroy

Advertisement

Too many ignored

I have long been disturbed by the lack of mental health services in Victoria.

We were promised replacement services when the institutions were closed, but instead people fall through the cracks and far too frequently end up in jail.

I shouldn’t know several people who have been attacked by someone who is mentally ill, but I do. I’ve longed for a political party to say they will build the services mentally ill people require, but election after election there has been no one to vote for.

It seems politicians prefer to put people in jail, with all the expense involved, instead of providing appropriate healthcare. Surely, it’s cheaper in the long run to provide care than have people in jail long term. Thirty years is far too long a wait, and too many people have been unnecessarily hurt, while too many have fallen through the cracks.

Eileen Ray, Ascot Vale Royal Park asylum

Notorious most of Victoria’s mental ″⁣asylums″⁣ certainly were, but under the reformist leadership of Dr E. Cunningham Dax and his chief clinical officer and successor, Dr Alan Stoller, in the 1950s and ’60s, Royal Park became an outstanding acute psychiatric hospital.

A dedicated staff and the successful introduction of new drugs restored many patients to mental health. Having reported extensively for The Age on Dax’s and Stoller’s work in the late 1950s, I have long felt that the closure of such a fine specialist facility to be a tragic mistake.

Claude Forell, Elwood Wilson’s Treaty pivot

One can only wonder when the leader of the Liberal Party who admitted she voted yes for the Voice, would scrap the Treaty as soon as she came to power. Listening to some of the members of the state Liberals and hearing of their far-right views, I can understand how she came to this decision so quickly.

Rod Oaten, North Carlton Going, going, gone

Obsessed with staying in power and the so-called ‘Big Build’, the previous Victorian Labor government are entirely the architects of their own doom.

Premiers Andrews and Allan ignored many of the everyday issues that Victorians wanted dealt with. The bigger social fabric improvements might have worked had the planning and implementation been fair, and there was no corruption.

To my mind, one subject of significance was the disinterest in an airport rail link. A second, is the arrogant “we know what’s best” planning policy that sought to bypass the views of local councils and residents. People object to bland ‘Eurobox’ apartments and the felling of every tree, mature, heritage or otherwise, being chopped and chipped.

Put simply, Labor forgot about looking after the issues that people care about, that make living worthwhile. There’s a real dilemma in where to place a vote: tick ALP and hope Ben Carroll rolls the dead wood and reshapes cabinet policy and future, or vote Liberal for no other reason than they’re not Labor.

Monica Lockheed, Brunswick East A fortunate life

No, Jess Wilson, I am not angry at the Labor Party as you say in your television ads. Living in Melbourne as an aged pensioner under a Labor government is a brilliant life. And, before I retired, Labor saved my small business during Covid and kept me from getting Covid myself.

I am old enough to remember that whenever we lose our Labor government, we lose so much more as well, whether it is our schools or our healthcare.

Joyce Sanders, North Melbourne

Advertisement

Labor’s heritage disdain

Integrity concerns under the Andrews and Allan governments are reason enough to reject Labor, but its destruction of Melbourne’s architectural heritage has sealed my vote.

Every day, Victorian-era buildings are reduced to rubble. No building dating from the 19th century through to the inter-war period should be demolished. Recently, Boroondara residents fought to save two 1880s–1890s homes designed by architect John Beswicke, only to see them torn down.

Through fast-tracked approvals, this government has stripped councils and residents of any say over their neighbourhoods, replacing heritage with inappropriate high-rises and no credible plan for infrastructure or liveability.

The government’s rhetoric on tourism and sustainability rings hollow. You cannot market a city’s charm while erasing its beauty, nor claim environmental credentials while demolishing durable historic structures—the greenest building is the one already standing.

Mignonne Rawson, Armadale What’s the big picture?

With less that a week to go, it was a relief to have at least one leader, the Greens leader Ellen Sandell speak, at least briefly, about two issues that have been completely absent in the campaigns and reporting so far. (“The accidental leader who negotiates with the premier and nude toddlers”, 23/11).

What do the major parties want Victoria to look like in ten, 20 and 50 years time? A highly educated, intelligent decentralised state or what? We simply don’t know.

As for nature conservation, we have a sense of Labor’s very confused view –protected native forests but still being logged, and continued duck shooting.

We have little idea of the Liberal, National and One Nations views.

Any chance our leaders could lift their eyes from potholes and crime. and give us their view of the big picture in the last week of the campaign?

Geoff Wescott, Northcote Re-writing the past

Your correspondent’s reflection (Letters, “Henry Higgins update”, 24/11) on the production My Fair Lady was interesting. But updating the lyrics, dialogue or ending to suit modern times surely conflicts with the purpose of the musical, and Shaw’s play Pygmalion, which was to reflect the societal attitudes of the era.

Of course, some of the lyrics and dialogue may cause offence to some people – that will be the case with any artwork. To change material in order to assuage current day sentiments is to effectively hide the past, whatever its perceived social failings. There is also the possibility that audiences in 2076 may find revisions reflecting 2026 values to be outdated - and want the revisions revised!

If revising material to suit modern gender relationships is to be enacted, the Bible would be the first volume needing revision. Beyond that tome, the list would be endless!

Brian Kidd, Mt Waverley To tell the truth

Why is there such a need to believe the unbelievable (″⁣Bigfoot paper trail fuels believers’ hopes″⁣, 24/11) and who cares if Bigfoot does exist?

There has been so much progress in technology, but there still isn’t a camera that will take clear photos of all of the unknowns, Bigfoot, UFOs and the Loch Ness monster, and yet we have millions of such photos of Santa.

Modern life is too confusing as indicated later in the sports pages where everyone knew about the sandpaper and yet almost no one did. We all want a simple life where people are honest, all newspapers report the truth, and politicians talk about what they are doing, rather than condemning the other side.

Dennis Fitzgerald, Box Hill AND ANOTHER THING

Advertisement

Photo: Matt Golding Molly Meldrum

Fell at the line and missed the AFL top 10 this year. Lost Warnie in 2022. Now Molly is gone. Haven’t Saints supporters suffered enough?

Don Hyatt, Dingley Village Australia’s Countdown versus UK’s Top of the Pops. Although it was not always clear what he was saying, Molly injected enthusiasm and pace. No contest against the Top of the Pops’ boring, formulaic grind.

Rob Willis, Newlands Arm Do yourself a favour! And for Molly, sing loud and clear, ″⁣Oh, when the Saints go marching in″⁣.

Myra Fisher, Brighton East Furthermore

Every time I see Jess Wilson brandishing her glossy covered action plan for Victoria, I picture it full of blank pages. We don’t hear details of her plan, and she doesn’t seem to answer questions.

Karen Dupleix, Brunswick

Advertisement

The article on the 1956 Olympic Games (22/11) included a reference to Donald Bradman, the cricketer. There was no such person. He was Don Bradman, or ‘the Don’, later becoming (reluctantly) Sir Donald Bradman – but never ‘Donald Bradman’.

Keith Tupper, Macleod Just when we thought it was safe to go into the water again when Trump’s influence had faded, Jensen Huang gets reinstated at Nvidia! The wounded shark is still out there.

Pam Cupper, Dimboola The reappearance of Jensen Huang has an absolutely clear message for one and all. Earn enough money for a company and they will let you do anything.

Carmel Boyle, Alfredton I’m astounded we can put men on the moon, land machinery on Mars, but fail dismally to locate Bigfoot-Sasquatch, Yowie and the Yeti!

Greg Bardin, Altona North I was despairing of ever reading some good news in The Age, when I saw the letter from Dingley, (24/11), about a good Samaritan helping an 83-year-old in trouble. Thank you, to the many kind people out there. And may we have more positive stories.

Margaret Collings, Anglesea The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

title: Inside the great homework debate dividing our teachers, parents and students
text:
Advertisement

Exclusive NationalNSWEducation Inside the great homework debate dividing our teachers, parents and students Christopher Harris November 24, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The reluctance of some NSW public schools to set homework is exacerbating social inequalities as more privileged parents seek out tutoring to address perceived gaps in their children’s education, according to new research. NSW schools have the power to decide whether to enforce homework, with a Department of Education policy document from 2012 stating “research regarding the value of homework is inconclusive”. Other academics have said homework doesn’t improve learning outcomes in primary school. Delia Suteja Yeboah sets her 8-year-old daughter Myla extra maths work at home. Louise Kennerley But those claims are challenged in a new paper from academics at Western Sydney University and UTS, which says homework helps build study routines and students’ ability to read and perform mathematical tasks quickly and easily. The authors said part of the problem with the hundreds of studies on homework is that its benefits were cumulative, often over years, so it was difficult to capture in academic research.

Advertisement

It is also difficult to separate academic outcomes associated with homework from other variables, such as a classroom teacher’s influence on a student. Related Article Education Why parents are calling for the return of primary school homework “Ensuring that students revise classwork and reinforce their conceptual understanding has compounding effects. This is also the case with the much-maligned rote learning,” the research said. “On balance, with certain caveats, the weight of research indicates that homework is beneficial.” The homework findings were part of a bigger research endeavour, Schooling, Parenting and Ethnicity: Asian Migration and Australian Education project, conducted by researchers across Western Sydney University and UTS as part of a three-year project.

Advertisement

It was prompted by a need to better understand the growing impact of Asian migrant families on Australian schooling. Lead researcher from Western Sydney University, Professor Megan Watkins, said repeated practice, particularly in the early years of school, helped students master what they had learnt, reducing cognitive load and allowing students to give greater attention to higher-order thinking. “Many parents were quite upset their children didn’t get more homework,” she said. A major study has challenged widely held beliefs about the benefits of homework. Dominic Lorrimer Researchers interviewed dozens of teachers, students and parents about attitudes at six primary schools across Sydney at varying levels of social disadvantage and ethnic backgrounds. Homework is just one prong of the major study, which also probed Asian parents’ attitudes towards Australian schooling as well as the impact of coaching centres and tutoring culture.

Advertisement

One teacher told the researchers: “Our kids are so bombarded with tutoring that they don’t need the homework.” But parents had a different view, enrolling their children in tutoring because of insufficient homework in schools. The sample size of 500 parents revealed 20 per cent of respondents of an Indian or Chinese background spent 60 minutes or more on homework each night, compared to less than 2 per cent of the respondents from an Anglo background. However, many teachers could see the benefits of homework despite the push against it. “[They] thrive on this extra homework, especially the Chinese students,” one teacher said. Another teacher also favourably viewed homework, but her principal thought it was of zero importance.

Advertisement

Related Article Sorry, your browser doesn't support embedded videos. Exclusive

Education Years ago, a primary school banned homework. Now it’s changed its mind While some parents who could afford it sent their child to tutoring, one mother took it on herself to develop extra school work, visiting education bookstores regularly and planning her own homework based on the term’s classroom activities. Students surveyed described their homework as “minimal and optional”; some said it was “too easy”. Of those who were not given homework, many felt they should have been. The research ultimately found a case for homework. “Clearly, when schools don’t provide homework, many parents and students look for alternatives, such as academic tutoring, further exacerbating inequalities within school communities,” it said.

Advertisement

A NSW Department of Education spokesperson said the homework policy referenced by the academics was outdated and current guidelines did not refer to “inconclusive” research. “Setting homework is a common expectation in NSW public schools,” the spokesman said. “Each school is required to develop homework guidelines that outline their approach and are tailored to the needs of their students.” Delia Suteja Yeboah came to Australia from Indonesia in the 1990s where she learnt the discipline of doing homework every day from kindergarten. “Whether you are rich, you are poor, you go to public school, private school, you are taught in the same similar discipline,” she said.

Advertisement

Her daughter Myla, 8, receives homework each week including a spelling list of 30 words. She adds a maths questionnaire every morning for her daughter to complete and quizzes her when they’re out of the house. Recently, at a sushi restaurant, she quizzed Myla on the cost of the bill based on how many plates they had consumed. “Now I understand as a parent that I need to be able to make it fun and make it practical,” she said. “When I was in Indonesia, the study was way harder.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. title: NSW leads in voluntary assisted dying but telehealth barriers persist
text:
Advertisement

NationalNSWEuthanasia NSW leads in voluntary assisted dying but telehealth barriers persist Jack Gramenz November 24, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. More people chose to end their lives in NSW under the state’s voluntary assisted dying (VAD) program than any other jurisdiction, but access for regional and rural applicants remains limited by an effective ban on telehealth. In the 12 months to the end of June this year, 1419 people died in NSW after administration of a voluntary assisted dying substance, an average of nearly four people per day and an increase of 38 per cent in the second full year of the state’s assisted dying program. NSW was the last state to introduce voluntary assisted dying. NSW MPs voting during the successful passage of the Voluntary Assisted Dying Bill in 2021. Dean Lewins / AAP The figures are contained in the NSW Voluntary Assisted Dying Board’s annual report, released on Monday. Advocacy group Go Gentle’s chief executive Linda Swan said it was expected NSW would have the most people dying in this way, as it has the highest population.

Advertisement

“Even so, VAD deaths account for a tiny proportion of all deaths in the state,” Swan said. Go Gentle chief executive Dr Linda Swan says forcing seriously unwell people to travel long distances for assessments is cruel and unnecessary. James Brickwood In Queensland, 1082 people died during the same reporting period, a slightly larger proportion of that state’s population. Victoria reported 780 deaths among people issued a permit, but 268 of those died without being administered a voluntary assisted dying substance. WA recorded 541 deaths. The ACT’s program began operating last year and the Northern Territory’s will begin in 2028.

Advertisement

Services in NSW are also well-funded in comparison to other jurisdictions and ensure people have access to multiple end-of-life options, Swan said. Related Article Vale Witty and warm, James Valentine lifted the spirits of a city “There is also a growing awareness of the VAD option, partially as a result of several recent high profile VAD deaths – James Valentine and Lex Marinos,” Swan said. But the chief executive of Right To Life UK said the NSW figures were deeply alarming. Alisdair Hungerford-Morgan urged against any expansion, calling for a review of the state’s system “including whether claimed safeguards in current legislation are protecting vulnerable people in practice”.

Advertisement

The state’s VAD board is an independent oversight body which decides whether people applying for access to voluntary assisted dying can access the program, among other functions. Advocates spread messages of support behind NSW Parliament during the campaign to legalise voluntary assisted dying. Nick Moir The report notes equity of access regardless of location is a key principle of the state’s laws and more than two-thirds of the 2875 initial assessments for access in the reporting period were for people outside the Greater Sydney area. Regional areas generally have older populations than major cities. Board chair Jenni Millbank said the board is an advocate for changing federal laws to remove “restrictions on the use of carriage services for steps in the voluntary assisted dying process that would otherwise be lawful and clinically appropriate to occur via audiovisual communication such as telehealth”. Swan said people looking to access telehealth were seriously unwell and in no condition to travel long distances for assessments.

Advertisement

“Expecting them to do so when an alternative exists in the form of telehealth is cruel and unnecessary. “This is about putting the needs of dying people first, rather than forcing them to navigate unnecessary barriers at the end of their lives,” Swan said. Because of a Federal Court ruling in 2023 that voluntary assisted dying is considered suicide, laws preventing the use of a carriage service (such as voice or video calls and emails) to incite or provide information about suicide have prevented doctors providing telehealth consults on euthanasia. It has also led to prolonged suffering for some, due to delays in accessing substances in some states where scripts had to be sent by mail rather than electronically. Health ministers from Victoria, South Australia, Tasmania, Western Australia and the ACT wrote to federal Health Minister Mark Butler and Attorney-General Michelle Rowland in October urging the laws be amended to allow for patients to be assessed for euthanasia via telehealth. “For many people in our states and territories, access to VAD is restricted by where they live,” the ministers wrote.

Advertisement

“This is an issue of equity.” Attorney-General Michelle Rowland speaking at Labor’s national conference in July. Dominic Lorrimer But NSW and Queensland did not join the call. Health Minister Ryan Park said changing the law was a federal responsibility but NSW supports eligible patients to access the scheme in all parts of the state. “The report shows voluntary assisted dying is meeting the needs of those who require it, and that its systems and processes are working effectively,” Park said.

Advertisement

“Ensuring safe and equitable access for all eligible people underpins the approach to voluntary assisted dying in NSW.” Labor Party members voted in July to amend the criminal code to allow telehealth assessments but also guaranteed MPs a conscience vote on the issue if it goes to parliament. Rowland cited concerns that changes could facilitate elder abuse and said it was “fundamentally a health policy issue”. Get alerts on breaking news as it happens. The Reserve Bank could be forced into cutting interest rates by the middle of next year to salvage the jobs market, one of the nation’s biggest lenders has predicted, while Chalmers flags savings in the public service to rein in government spending. As Opposition Leader Angus Taylor declared the Coalition could return to power next year because the government had mismanaged the economy, the ANZ became the first major commercial bank to predict the RBA would have to reverse its aggressive monetary policy stance due to the deteriorating economic outlook. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Treasurer Dr Jim Chalmers and Minister for Small Business, Minister for International Development, and Minister for Multicultural Affairs Dr Anne Aly Alex Ellinghausen On Tuesday, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese talked up Labor’s preparation for the next election in a caucus meeting, while the Liberal leader projected optimism to beat a government that is “on the rocks” and could head to the polls next year. “Make no mistake about it, colleagues: we can win the next election,” Taylor told a partyroom meeting. The next election is not due until May 2028 and the prime minister is not expected to call an early poll.

Advertisement

On Monday, Treasurer Jim Chalmers said his upcoming mid-year budget update would reveal a grim economic outlook with inflation likely to remain elevated until the second half of next year, unemployment above 5 per cent and larger budget deficits from 2027-28. He said a series of factors, including the spike in oil prices, the AI construction boom and higher interest rates were all weighing on the economy, which will be smaller than forecast in the May budget. Chalmers told ABC’s 7.30 on Tuesday that the government was looking for savings in the “efficiency of the public service”. Two weeks ago, this masthead reported Labor would examine public service cuts as well as winding back generous subsidies for batteries and EVs, which Chalmers also appeared to confirm. “Obviously, we’ll have to look at some of the programs which have been quite successful to make sure that they’re sustainable,” he said. “We’ll have to look at the efficiency of the public service, and in other areas.”

Advertisement

Figures to be released on Wednesday are expected to show inflation in October jumping from 4.3 per cent to almost 5 per cent because of last month’s large jump in oil prices. Related Article Federal budget ‘No use pretending otherwise’: Chalmers warns of tough year ahead as jobless and inflation forecasts worsen ANZ’s head of Australian economics, Adam Boyton, said it was clear the jobs market was weakening more than expected. He said a higher unemployment rate plus the growing evidence of a slowdown across the property market, including signs that advertised rents are starting to fall, meant the RBA would likely start considering a rate cut by June. The Reserve on a 6-3 vote earlier this month lifted the cash rate to an 18-year high of 4.85 per cent. “We are bringing forward our timing for the first RBA rate cut to June 2027. We then expect a follow-up cut in August, taking the cash rate to 4.35 per cent. A further easing in early 2028 will bring the cash rate to 4.1 per cent,” he said.

Advertisement

A rate cut in June, after an increase in November, would be one of the shortest turnarounds in monetary policy this century. The smallest gap was five months between December 2001, when the RBA cut interest rates, and May the following year when it started to lift borrowing costs. When the Reserve raised rates this month, it expected oil prices to average almost $US110 a barrel to December and then ease to $US95 a barrel. But in a positive development for the global and domestic economy, oil has dropped by almost 24 per cent since late October. It fell below $US89 a barrel on Tuesday. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has told colleagues they can win the next federal election. Dominic Lorrimer That is already feeding into petrol prices, with the average across the nation’s major capital cities falling from $2.40 a litre in late October to a two-month low of $2.05 a litre last week.

Advertisement

Chalmers has said in a bid to further reduce inflation pressures his budget update will include “budget-sized” savings, suggesting reductions worth billions of dollars. Pressure to curb inflation has pushed Labor away from one-off subsidies, such as electricity rebates, toward more targeted cost-of-living relief. Reprising its 2025 election playbook, and aiming to capitalise on a remaining area of strength against the Coalition as its overall polling position fades, Labor is planning to lean into its healthcare agenda next year. Related Article Opinion

Federal budget Tasmania’s economy is going south, and it will hit the hip pockets of every Australian Shane Wright Senior economics correspondent Following Monday’s freeze of the $25 medicine co-payment, upcoming announcements are expected on lower specialist fees, boosted regional bulk-billing, and expanded roles for pharmacists and allied health workers.

Advertisement

“We’ve still got a big lead on the Coalition in health, so we will lean in next year,” one senior source said. In lifting interest rates, the Reserve Bank has noted the impact of federal and state government spending adding to demand across the economy which has helped fuel the nation’s inflationary pressures. Analysis released by S&P Global on Tuesday said state government spending and debt would continue to grow. By 2030, state debt is now expected to reach $980 billion, up almost a third from $739 billion today. That surge in debt will push up the share of state budgets used to cover interest repayments. Almost 10 per cent of Victoria’s budget will be spent on interest by the end of the decade, with every other state bar WA spending at least 6 per cent. Treasurer Jim Chalmers during question time on Tuesday November 24. Dominic Lorrimer

The ramp-up in state spending is not being driven by NSW or Victoria where expenditure on major projects is expected to ease over coming years. S&P noted that states like South Australia and Queensland – under pressure over the Brisbane Olympics – are “enthusiastically” opening their purse strings. On Tuesday, the Tasmanian government revealed the expected cost of its planned football stadium had increased by $100 million over the past 12 months to $1.23 billion. It had originally been expected to cost $715 million. S&P Global lead analyst Martin Foo said the states were under growing financial pressure. “Australian state budgets are already stretched. In 2027, housing prices and property-related tax revenue could fall even further, while swelling interest costs will heap on more pressure,” he said.

“With collective debt heading towards $1 trillion by 2031, debt-servicing costs will steadily crowd out spending on public services and infrastructure.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

Amazon cameras were kept away from Justin Langer’s passionate rebuke of the Australian team for toying with the idea of using red frog lollies to illegally shine the ball in their first Test match after the Sandpapergate scandal. Sources with knowledge of the 2018 tour of the UAE, where Australia played two Tests against Pakistan, have confirmed recollections published by broadcaster Gerard Whateley that there was a discussion about using sugar-based sweets to keep the ball shiny in the first Test of the series in Dubai. Justin Langer addresses the media in the UAE in 2018. Getty Images The lollies of choice were red frogs, used typically to help with players’ sugar levels in hot conditions, but at the time forbidden from being taken onto the field because of the team’s hyper sensitivity to bad optics after the South Africa tour earlier in 2018. The use of mints or other sugar-based sweets as an adjunct to saliva had been a common practice in cricket for decades, despite being outlawed as an artificial substance being used on the ball. Saliva was banned outright from being used on the ball amid the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 and players are now restricted to using perspiration only.

Advertisement

Langer makes a point to players in the UAE eight years ago. Getty Images The Amazon documentary series known as The Test has become a recurring part of the national team’s story over the past eight years, and a fourth season is currently being filmed. It was conceived partly to allow access to a dressing room that had previously been a closed shop, and partly to showcase the team’s new direction. But its rules of engagement include the team always having the option of having veto over what is recorded or ultimately broadcast. Countless confidential team discussions have been left on the cutting room floor or not recorded, and a source told this masthead that Langer’s rebuttal of ball tampering was one of them. Loading This masthead has also confirmed that bowlers Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc, Pat Cummins and Nathan Lyon jointly indicated they were not prepared to take responsibility for the ball tampering plot because they felt that David Warner was the architect.

Advertisement

Whateley quoted one member of the quartet as saying: “F---k Davey, we are not going down for that guy.” A source close to the bowlers told this masthead on condition of anonymity that the accuracy of the quote may be disputed, but the overall sentiment is right. The relational chasm between Warner and the bowlers has never quite healed since, and has only grown wider lately. Warner declined to comment when approached by this masthead. Australia in the field during the Dubai Test in 2018. Ryan Pierse/Getty Images Langer’s infuriated response to the floating of ideas about artificially altering the condition of the ball is a reminder that it took Australian cricket a while to reconfigure itself after the sandpaper episode.

Advertisement

Before the recent South Africa Test series, Travis Head told this masthead that he had similarly stamped out discussions about ball tampering in the South Australian dressing room. Head made his Test debut for Australia in the UAE Test match where the subject came up. “I made a pretty strong stand at that point, and I was captain at the time, that they weren’t going to be in the dressing room if that’s the case, if that’s what [they want to do],” Head said last month. “I didn’t care what other teams did. I didn’t care if we were facing it. “I just knew what a couple of close friends had gone through, and knew what the [Australian] team had gone through, and the flow-on effect of that. I don’t care if we’re bottom of the table, as long as we play the game the right way. That was my opinion, and still is my opinion.” Editor's pick Updated

Ball tampering ‘We all knew’: Bancroft claims entire Australian team was aware sandpaper use in South Africa Head also reiterated something that Cricket Australia concluded last week - the team’s improved sense of perspective about playing the game in the right way has been largely driven by skipper Cummins.

Advertisement

“It’s driven from Pat. Pat’s always said it’s a game, and it’s not do or die,” Head said. “If South Africa play really, really well, and we lose 3-0, that’s OK; it’s not the end of the world. We’ll wake up tomorrow. I think that then brings in, I guess, that freer side of yourself to go out and express yourself. “We’ve seen other teams around the world hold on to certain things or think it’s the most important thing they’re ever going to do, and sometimes you can play on that. You can see that they get tense and feel pressure, and you never play better when you’re tense and feel pressured.” Related Article Australian cricket Paine the peacemaker: Ex-skipper looms as key figure in Sandpapergate talks CA declined to comment on Whateley’s investigation, but the governing body is working to finalise terms of reference for the “truth forum” to be conducted to allow members of the 2018 South African tour party to share their often conflicting recollections. “It meant a lot to speak with David and Todd on Friday. Being Australian captain carries with it an awesome responsibility,” Cummins said last week after meeting with chair David Boon and chief executive Todd Greenberg.

title: How Bluey exported Brisbane to viewers who didn’t think its setting was real
text:

NationalQueenslandCityChats How Bluey exported Brisbane to viewers who didn’t think its setting was real Nick Dent , Dominique Tassell and Neesha Sinnya November 24, 2026 — 7:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.
